items.title: Stewart Copeland announces 2027 ‘Police Deranged for Orchestra’ world tour
items.summary: Stewart Copeland announces a 2027 world tour performing 'Police Deranged for Orchestra', celebrating his 75th birthday and The Police's 50th anniversary.
items.fullText:
Stewart Copeland, drummer of The Police, has announced a 2027 world tour performing “Police Deranged for Orchestra,” his orchestral reworking of the band’s catalog. The tour runs from March through September 2027 across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Iceland and Australia. Copeland is billing it as a joint celebration of his 75th birthday and the 50th anniversary of The Police, which he formed in 1977. UK presale tickets opened on 26 November 2026 with the code PDO2027, ahead of general on-sale on 27 November 2026. Further ticket and presale details are listed at stewartcopeland.net.

“Police Deranged for Orchestra” sets Police songs including “Roxanne,” “Every Breath You Take,” “Don’t Stand So Close to Me” and “Every Little Thing She Does Is Magic” for symphony orchestra, backed by a rock band and vocalists. Copeland has toured the program with orchestras since 2021, and a studio recording of the arrangements was released on 23 June 2023. The project grew out of “Everyone Stares: The Police Inside Out,” Copeland’s 2006 documentary built from Super 8 footage he shot on tour with the band.

About Stewart Copeland

Stewart Armstrong Copeland was born on 16 July 1952 in Alexandria, Virginia. His family moved to Cairo within months of his birth and later to Beirut, where he grew up. In early 1977, he formed The Police in London with Sting and guitarist Henry Padovani, who was replaced soon after by Andy Summers. The band’s debut single, “Fall Out,” appeared on Illegal Records in 1977, followed by the albums “Outlandos d’Amour” (1978), “Reggatta de Blanc” (1979), “Zenyatta Mondatta” (1980), “Ghost in the Machine” (1981) and “Synchronicity” (1983). The Police were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2003 and reunited for a 151-date anniversary tour between May 2007 and August 2008, closing with a show at Madison Square Garden in New York. In 2023, Side-Line covered the “Police Diaries” deluxe reissue gathering pre-Police demos, and in 2016 reported on the half-speed remastering of The Police’s catalog at Abbey Road Studios.

Beyond The Police, Copeland has built a parallel career scoring film and television, including Francis Ford Coppola’s “Rumble Fish” (1983), which brought him a Golden Globe nomination, and “Wall Street” (1987). He has also recorded with the bands Animal Logic (formed 1989, with Stanley Clarke and Deborah Holland), Oysterhead (formed 2000, with Les Claypool and Trey Anastasio) and Gizmodrome (formed 2005, reformed in 2017 with Adrian Belew, Vittorio Cosma and Mark King). His stage works include the operas “The Tell-Tale Heart” (Long Beach Opera, 2013) and “Electric Saint” (Deutsches Nationaltheater und Staatskapelle Weimar, 2021), and the ballets “King Lear” (San Francisco Ballet) and “Noah’s Ark/Solcheeka” (Seattle Symphony). His 2021 album “Divine Tides,” made with Ricky Kej, won Best Immersive Audio Album at the 65th Grammy Awards in February 2023, his seventh Grammy.

“Police Deranged for Orchestra” has been Copeland’s main touring vehicle since 2021, pairing his orchestral arrangements of The Police’s songbook with a rock band and vocalists. The 2027 dates mark the production’s first confirmed world tour, timed to his 75th birthday and the band’s 50th anniversary.

items.title: “Will We Grow or Decay?” — Rose Chamber Stare Down a Dying Society in Video for “Modern Rot”
items.summary: You need no sympathy to understand what I say We’re a dying society. Falling, being swept away There are mornings when the present feels bleaker than any future you used… The post “Will We Grow or Decay?” — Rose Chamber Stare Down a Dying Society in Video for
items.fullText:
You need no sympathy to understand what I say
We’re a dying society. Falling, being swept away

There are mornings when the present feels bleaker than any future you used to worry about. Before breakfast, you can read a dispatch from a bombed hospital, see someone ask strangers for help with rent, and have your stolen data trigger a targeted ad promising a full night’s sleep. You put the phone down because you’ve had enough and pick it up again because, like a Pavlovian dog, you are dying to know what the next tragedy is. That impulse gets a blunt diagnosis in Modern Rot, the opening track and first single from Rose Chamber’s debut album, My Silhouette.

The track takes its time getting to the dance floor. A bell tolls through the opening synth tones as a drum hit echoes and a guitar squeals in the distance. A woman’s sampled voice comes through just before the darkwave beat and bass synth take over. The guitar holds a few low notes over the beat until they have the resonance of a piano with the sustain pedal down, reminiscent of “The Lord’s Prayer” by The Lords of the New Church. Vocalist Ace Stallings sings with Ian McKaye’s hardcore bite and Glenn Danzig’s full-throated force, with Kevin Iavaroni of New Jersey’s The Shape contributing guest vocals.

Evan Schlomann opens his video with Stallings standing stoically, his glasses shadowed, hands clasped, and face starkly lit against a black background. The shot holds for nearly half a minute before the bright neck of a guitar cuts across the frame. Then the images start to overlap. A second face appears behind the first, and late in the clip the guitar crosses the singer’s chest even as both hands go to his head. There’s a particular unease to watching one person become several while the song asks what’s going to happen to all of us.

Watch the video for Modern Rot below:

Stallings and Schlomann formed Rose Chamber in 2024 after the end of a crossover band, drawing on their shared interest in darkwave and synth music. They come out of hardcore, punk, and metal, with Sentinel in their past and Wretched Rite, Eliminators, and Mutually Assured Destruction among their current bands.

Raven Records issued the duo’s first cassette, State of Affairs, in early 2024. A year later, they shared the Double Feature split tape with The Shape on Death Eternal. My Silhouette brings together the material from both tapes with six new tracks.

My Silhouette (AV!106) is out January 22, 2027 via Avant! Records, with a U.S. co-release from Phage Tapes. The album will be available digitally and on neon-green vinyl in a run of 300 LPs, each with a lyric insert. Pre-order or pre-save the album here.

items.title: Morten Harket – Human Grace (Digital/CD/Vinyl Album – Warner Music)
items.summary: János Janurik reviews Morten Harket's new solo album "Human Grace," out 27 November 2026 via Warner Music, track by track.
items.fullText:
Norwegian singer Morten Harket released his seventh solo album, “Human Grace,” on 27 November 2026 through Warner Music, on digital, CD and vinyl. János Janurik reviews the album for Side-Line.

For some time now, Morten Harket has been making headlines again. Part of the reason, of course, is his new solo album, “Human Grace,” due for release on November 27. But the attention surrounding the Norwegian singer is not solely about the extraordinary instrument he carries in his throat. It is also about the insidious neurological condition that has affected his body: Parkinson’s disease. Morten has spoken openly about his health problems, including the fact that the illness had already become part of his life long before most fans had any idea that something might be wrong with their beloved singer.

But if you would rather not feel sorry for him – and I suspect that is not what Morten himself would want either – my advice is simple: get hold of “Human Grace,” settle into your favourite armchair or onto the sofa, and surrender to the magic of the music and that still unmistakable voice. Thanks to the record label, I have already had the privilege of experiencing this for myself. And yet I find myself wanting to return to it again and again, letting the music wrap itself around my soul like a soothing balm.

Outside, snow is falling quietly. Inside, where the soul resides, Morten Harket’s voice offers reassurance: there will be another spring, another summer, and life is still something to be loved. Even when it does not always treat us kindly.

With that in mind, here are some thoughts on the album’s outstanding moments. Fortunately, there are plenty of them. The record contains ten songs, and each has something to offer.

Ten songs, ten different worlds

This nearly forty-minute musical journey opens with the title track and a guitar motif that immediately hits home, at once melancholic and uplifting. Then Morten’s voice enters, and from that moment on, it has our undivided attention. He reflects on the troubled state of the world, while also expressing gratitude for all the joyful moments life has brought him and holding on to the hope of meeting again in eternity. But don’t expect a gloomy lament. This could easily have been a powerful a-ha song. For now, though, it is “just” Morten, standing on his own, facing the world with the dignity and elegance suggested by the song’s title.

That sense of solitude does not last long. On the second track, already familiar to many listeners, Morten is joined by his daughter Tomine Harket, who is a singer and voice actress in her own right. “Hold Me” is one of the most beautiful moments on the album.

“Won’t you hold me? And everything loses its weight. So hold me close, and the darkness leaves this place.”

Father and daughter sing these lines together, and it makes you want to reach out and hug Morten, too. Not as an overzealous fan, but simply to let him know that we need him – his music, his voice.

The family affair continues with the next track. On “Falling Down,” Karmen Poppi A. Harket joins her father. Once again, we arrive at a simple but comforting thought: there should always be a hand ready to catch us when we begin to fall. It is another beautiful father-daughter conversation, expressed through music.

Track four is one of my personal favourites, perhaps not entirely unrelated to my own Depeche Mode obsession. Gritty guitars, punchy drums and a dark, growling bass bring to mind the atmosphere of “Walking in My Shoes.” Somewhere in the background, an instrument wails like a siren, and Morten sounds particularly convincing in this angrier role. Especially when his voice comes through what sounds like a police megaphone: “Is this really what you want?” he asks us. “Lord, I Can’t Help You Now” may be the first song on the album in which we begin to sense a certain resignation.

A fragile acoustic opening introduces “Now Your Heart Is Broken,” almost as if it were the aftermath of the previous song. Its simplicity brings Simon & Garfunkel to mind. The real moment of weightlessness arrives about a minute and a half in, when the strings join the acoustic guitar. As the violins begin to soar, we find ourselves flying with them, while feeling that a little piece of our own hearts has broken, too. Morten’s vocal performance is particularly vulnerable here.

The title “Shot of Fear” had already caught my attention. After hearing it, the song quickly became one of my favourites. Morten’s voice seems to float somewhere in the ether, reaching those heights that only he can reach, singing in a way that is unmistakably his. This dramatic track could almost be a sibling of “Forever Not Yours.” For me, it is one of the album’s high points. And then there is that guitar towards the end, accompanied by the strings in the background. If this doesn’t break your heart, perhaps you don’t have one. The song also leaves us with a wonderfully poetic image: “You’re lying down softly on a bed of grass, you’re with me, we don’t have a past.”

“Did I Leave You Behind” begins with a similarly acoustic intro. Morten asks us to keep him in our memories, and his voice reaches for the heights once again as he sings the chorus. At the same time, he repeats, with the calm wisdom of a stoic philosopher, that sometimes we simply need more time. It could sound like a cliché, but somehow it doesn’t. This is poetry, music from another sphere, carried by an almost angelic voice.

We are gradually approaching the end of the album, but there are still more highlights to come. One of them is “What Is It You Want With Me,” which opens with melancholy brass, a steady, almost monotonous drum pattern and a restrained guitar. It feels as though a funeral procession is passing before us. For a moment, you might even think Morten is singing his own obituary. Is he addressing the woman he loves? Or is he speaking to us, the listeners? The whispered passage towards the end is particularly haunting. But no, this is not the farewell just yet.

Compared with the previous track, “The Old Church” begins almost as if the sun were chasing away the clouds. Perhaps something similar was happening inside the singer while he was writing and recording these songs. It unfolds a simple image, both musically and lyrically. Around the one-and-a-half-minute mark, it takes on an almost gospel-like feel, inviting us to stand up, clap our hands and praise something greater than ourselves. No, Morten is not trying to convert anyone. Yet there is something spiritual about this song, something that goes beyond its title. No church pomp, no noise from the outside world – the kind of noise in which we sometimes can no longer even hear our own voices. Every now and then, we all need the quiet of an inner sanctuary.

The closing track, which is also the current single, continues this process of self-examination. Morten sings about longing, inner courage, the hope of starting over and the need to be understood. “I would be the man you wanted” – coming from a man in his late sixties, this is a beautiful confession. It also touches a listener in his early fifties who sometimes worries that he can no longer express his love and affection quite as well as he would like to. But there is another line, too: “I would listen when you can’t explain.” Perhaps that is one of the most important things in any human relationship. And once again, we find the vulnerability, dignity and kindness that were already present in the opening title track. These are things every individual needs, and humanity as a whole, too.

There will be another spring

The snow is still falling outside. I don’t know whether it will last until Christmas. But even if it doesn’t, I hope “Human Grace” will find its way under the Christmas trees of people who approach music with open ears, open hearts, open minds and open souls.

Morten Harket himself has described the album as a celebration of life. It is about love and human connection. What better message could there be for Christmas?

Tracklist

  1. “Human Grace”
  2. “Hold Me” (feat. Tomine Harket)
  3. “Falling Down” (feat. Karmen Poppi A. Harket)
  4. “Lord, I Can’t Help You Now”
  5. “Now Your Heart Is Broken”
  6. “Shot of Fear”
  7. “Did I Leave You Behind”
  8. “What Is It You Want With Me”
  9. “The Old Church”
  10. “If I Ever See Your Face Again”

“Human Grace” is available on black vinyl, beige vinyl, CD and digital formats through Warner Music, including a D2C-exclusive beige gatefold vinyl through Warner’s own store.

About Morten Harket

Morten Harket was born on 14 September 1959 in Kongsberg, Norway. He formed a-ha in Oslo in 1982 with Magne Furuholmen and Pål Waaktaar, and the band’s breakthrough single “Take On Me” reached number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 in October 1985 from the album “Hunting High and Low.” Alongside a-ha, Harket has released six prior solo albums: “Poetenes Evangelium” (1993), “Wild Seed” (1995), “Vogts Villa” (1996), “Letter from Egypt” (2008), “Out of My Hands” (2012) and “Brother” (2014). He has also acted, including the “Kamilla og tyven” films (1988-1989) and “Yohan: The Child Wanderer” (2009), and was made a Knight of the Order of St. Olav in 2012 for his contribution to Norwegian music. A-ha’s most recent studio album remains “True North” (2022).

“Human Grace” is Harket’s seventh solo album, released twelve years after “Brother.” It was built from demos and studio recordings made in the years since that album, with some material newly arranged and produced for the release. The ten-track record features Harket’s daughters Tomine Harket and Karmen Poppi A. Harket as guest vocalists, on “Hold Me” and “Falling Down” respectively. Peter Kvint co-produced and co-wrote eight of the ten songs, Ole Sverre Olsen wrote lyrics for six tracks, Jonas Kroon mixed the album and Erik Ljunggren oversaw post-production, with contributions from the Stockholm Studio Orchestra and Swedish and Norwegian session musicians.

Harket disclosed his Parkinson’s disease diagnosis in June 2025, explaining that the condition has affected his ability to control his voice. Much of “Human Grace” was recorded before the diagnosis, with overdubs added between July 2025 and July 2026. Side-Line first reported on “Human Grace” when it was announced in September 2026, alongside an interview with Harket about the album, his voice and a-ha’s future.

items.title: Trevor Horn & His Band confirm concert at The Assembly in Royal Leamington Spa
items.summary: Producer and musician Trevor Horn will play The Assembly in Royal Leamington Spa on 3 December 2026, part of the venue's 100th-anniversary concert series.
items.fullText:
English record producer and musician Trevor Horn will perform with his band at The Assembly in Royal Leamington Spa on 3 December 2026, part of the venue’s concert series marking its 100th anniversary. Tickets are available through AGMP Concerts and Seetickets.

Horn formed The Buggles with Geoff Downes in 1978. Their single “Video Killed The Radio Star” reached No. 1 in the UK in September 1979, and its video became the first to air on MTV in August 1981. He went on to produce ABC’s “The Lexicon Of Love” (1982) and Yes’ “90125” (1983), whose single “Owner Of A Lonely Heart” gave Yes their only US No. 1, as well as Frankie Goes To Hollywood’s No. 1 singles “Relax,” “Two Tribes” and “The Power Of Love,” after signing the band as the first act on ZTT Records, the label he co-founded with Jill Sinclair and journalist Paul Morley in 1983.

Horn also produced albums and singles for Tina Turner, Tom Jones, Barry Manilow, Cher, Boyzone, Lisa Stansfield and Robbie Williams, and Seal’s 1991 debut album, whose single “Kiss From A Rose” won him a Grammy Award in 1995. The Leamington Spa concert will draw on material from across his career as a producer, performer and songwriter.

Trevor Horn & His Band at The Assembly

  • 3 December 2026, The Assembly, Royal Leamington Spa
  • Part of the venue’s 100th-anniversary concert series
  • Tickets via AGMP Concerts and Seetickets

About Trevor Horn

Trevor Charles Horn was born on 15 July 1949 in Hetton-le-Hole, County Durham, England, and grew up in Durham City. He took up double bass as a child and later taught himself bass guitar, playing in bands including the Outer Limits and Nick North and Northern Lights, whose members included Geoff Downes and Tina Charles.

Horn and Downes formed The Buggles in 1978. Their debut single, “Video Killed The Radio Star,” reached No. 1 in the UK in September 1979, and its video became the first to air on MTV when the channel launched in August 1981. Horn joined Yes as lead singer in 1980 for the album “Drama” and its tour, and later returned to the band as producer for “90125” (1983) and “Big Generator” (1987); he also produced the band’s 2011 album “Fly From Here.”

In 1983, Horn and Jill Sinclair bought Basing Street Studios in London, renamed it Sarm West Studios, and co-founded ZTT Records with journalist Paul Morley. The label’s first signing was Frankie Goes To Hollywood, whose singles “Relax,” “Two Tribes” and “The Power Of Love” all reached No. 1 in the UK under Horn’s production. ZTT’s roster also included German synth-pop group Propaganda, who signed to the label in 1983 and released their debut album “A Secret Wish.” The same year, Horn co-formed Art of Noise, co-writing “Close (To The Edit),” “Beat Box,” “Moments In Love” and “Slave To The Rhythm.”

Horn produced ABC’s “The Lexicon Of Love” in 1982 and Yes’ “90125” in 1983, the album that gave Yes their only US No. 1 single with “Owner Of A Lonely Heart.” His other production credits include albums and singles for Tina Turner, Tom Jones, Barry Manilow, Cher, Boyzone, Lisa Stansfield and Robbie Williams. He produced Seal’s 1991 debut album, which reached No. 1 in the UK, and its single “Kiss From A Rose,” which won Horn a Grammy Award in 1995. His later production work includes Mike Oldfield’s “Tubular Bells II” (1992), Belle and Sebastian’s “Dear Catastrophe Waitress” (2003) and LeAnn Rimes’ “Can’t Fight The Moonlight,” a No. 1 in the UK and Australia.

Horn has won three Brit Awards for Best British Producer (1983, 1985 and 1992), the Ivor Novello Award for Outstanding Contribution to British Music (2010) and two Grammy Awards, for Yes’ “90125” and Seal’s “Kiss From A Rose.” He received the Music Producers Guild’s Lifetime Achievement Award in 2014 and was appointed CBE in the 2011 New Year Honours. Horn released “Trevor Horn Reimagines The Eighties” in 2019, toured with Dire Straits Legacy between 2018 and 2020, and published the memoir “Adventures In Modern Recording: From ABC To ZTT” in 2022. The Assembly concert on 3 December 2026 follows his dates on Seal’s 2023 tour.

items.title: HAAi confirms US DJ dates in late November and December 2026
items.summary: Australian-born, London-based DJ and producer HAAi will play US dates from 27 November to 6 December 2026, following her album "DIGITiSE" on Mute.
items.fullText:
Australian-born, London-based producer and DJ HAAi will play US dates from 27 November to 6 December 2026, across Los Angeles, San Francisco, Miami, Atlanta and New York, following the October release of her third studio album, “DIGITiSE,” on Mute.

HAAi describes “DIGITiSE” as the “bigger, ravey sibling” of her 2025 album “HUMANiSE,” saying the new record “holds the hand of HUMANiSE and walks it to the club.” The album brings in new collaborators Echonomist and Skybreak alongside Cantoalegre, a children’s choir from Medellín, Colombia, as well as past collaborators Pat Alvarez, ILA, James Massiah and Kaiden Ford.

US DJ dates for HAAi

  • 27 November – Los Angeles, CA – Time Warp LA at Ace * Mission Studios
  • 28 November – San Francisco, CA – Polyglamorous x Squish at The Great Northern
  • 3 December – Miami, FL – Raw Cuts, b2b with salute, at The Ground Club Space
  • 4 December – Atlanta, GA – Pisces
  • 5 December – New York, NY – FIXED at Good Room
  • 6 December – Miami, FL – Factory Basel closing night, b2b with Coffintexts, at Factory Town

HAAi’s schedule continues into 2027 with further international dates, including Fabric at Truth Club in Johannesburg on 15 January, the Castle of Good Hope in Cape Town on 16 January, Polari at FVTVR in Paris on 19 February, and three shows alongside The Avalanches in Australia: the Royal Botanic Gardens in Melbourne on 5 March, a show on the banks in Brisbane on 6 March, and the Sydney Opera House on 7 March.

About HAAi

HAAi is an Australian-born, London-based producer, songwriter and DJ. She released her debut album, “Baby, We’re Ascending,” before issuing her “DJ-Kicks” compilation in 2023, the same year as “Lights Out,” her collaboration with Fred again.. and Romy. Her second studio album, “HUMANiSE,” followed in October 2025 and was named among the year’s albums of the year by Rough Trade, Disco Pogo and Resident. HAAi founded UNiSON, a community-focussed club night in London, in 2024. Her third studio album, “DIGITiSE,” was released in October 2026 on Mute, and the November-December 2026 US dates mark her first club run in the country since the album’s release.

items.title: Ella Boh announces ‘mannequin’ EP for February 2027
items.summary: Los Angeles dark pop artist Ella Boh announces her EP "mannequin" for 23 February 2027 and releases the single "warning label" with a video.
items.fullText:
Los Angeles-based dark pop artist Ella Boh announced her next EP, “mannequin,” for release on 23 February 2027 via Bamboo Artists. Alongside the announcement, Boh released the new single “warning label” together with an official music video directed by Sophie Gallagher.

Pre-orders for “mannequin” are open now through Boh’s online store, including a standard and a limited-edition vinyl pressing. “Warning label” is streaming digitally, including on Spotify and Apple Music.

Boh described “warning label” as a song about recognising manipulation in a relationship: “When you want to see the good in someone, it becomes dangerously easy to be manipulated, especially when they know exactly what you wanna hear. ‘Warning label’ is about the psychological warfare of loving someone who constantly drains you. Being chewed up and spit out so many times that you can’t tell up from down. Wishing for a blatant, constant reminder, like a warning label on their forehead, to protect yourself from the person you love.”

The release follows Boh’s headline North American tour, which wrapped at the end of October. The run came close to selling out across its dates, and the VIP meet-and-greet package for the full tour sold out in advance.

About Ella Boh

Ella Boh is a dark pop artist based in Los Angeles, writing, producing and recording her own material. She began her career as a songwriter, working with artists including Selena Gomez, Jai Wolf and Freya Skye, before releasing her own debut project, “milk & honey.” She followed it with the “BLURRY DELUXE” EP, led by the singles “SERiAL KiLLER,” “BLOODY MARY” and “PRETTY BABY,” which has drawn more than 12.4 million Spotify streams and contributes to a catalogue Boh’s team puts at more than 75 million lifetime streams. Boh toured North America in support of her “BLURRY” era alongside Artemas and Ari Abdul. “mannequin,” due 23 February 2027 on Bamboo Artists, follows that run and the release of lead single “warning label.”

items.title: Nerisah release debut single ‘East Ghost’
items.summary: Paris duo Nerisah released their debut single "East Ghost" on 30 October 2026, recorded in Paris and mixed by Andreas Lecter.
items.fullText:
Paris-based duo Nerisah released their debut single, “East Ghost,” digitally on 30 October 2026. Formed in March 2026 by Bosnian-born vocalist Mersiha Husagic and French musician Nicolas Rabine, the duo combine spectral vocals, echoing guitars and non-traditional percussion into a sound the pair describe as “nocturnal dust, with a taste of alternative rock.” They sing in French, English and Bosnian.

Husagic and Rabine met at an open mic at the Highlander bar in Paris, where they first performed together before forming the project. The pair cite recordings from the 1950s through the 1990s as a reference point for the track’s raw, unpolished sound. For percussion on “East Ghost,” they used cowbells and tambourines instead of a conventional drum kit.

Husagic wrote “East Ghost” several years before Nerisah formed, during a period when news coverage of war brought back memories of her childhood in Bosnia. She later reworked the song with Rabine, who added guitar, synth and lyre parts. Describing the song’s origin, she said: “I was alone a lot at that time and felt quite lost. Holding a guitar gave me comfort. What began as a personal refuge gradually became a shared creation when Nico added his guitar, giving the song a new life and opening it up to unexpected possibilities.”

Husagic and Rabine produced “East Ghost” themselves. The track was recorded by engineers Andreas Lecter, Bernard Natier and Bénédicte Schmitt at Montmartre Recording, Studio Garage and Labomatic Studios in Paris, and mixed and mastered by Lecter at Studio Montmartre Recording. An official video for the track, directed and edited by Husagic with colour grading by Rabine, is available on YouTube.

“East Ghost” is available digitally on Bandcamp, Spotify, Apple Music and SoundCloud.

About Nerisah

Nerisah is a Paris-based duo formed in March 2026 by Bosnian-born singer, guitarist and percussionist Mersiha Husagic and French multi-instrumentalist Nicolas Rabine. The pair met at an open mic at the Highlander bar in Paris, where a shared performance led to a recurring creative partnership built on improvisation. Husagic and Rabine write, produce and record their own material, drawing on 1950s-to-1990s recording aesthetics and an unconventional approach to arrangement. “East Ghost,” released on Bandcamp on 30 October 2026, is the duo’s debut single and first commercially released recording.

items.title: Erasure interview: Ewan McLaren on his fan history book ‘All Through the Years’
items.summary: An interview with Ewan McLaren, author of All Through the Years: A Fan’s History of...
items.fullText:
An interview with Ewan McLaren, author of All Through the Years: A Fan’s History of Erasure, 1985–2026

Despite Erasure’s remarkable career spanning more than four decades, the story of the British duo has rarely been explored in book form. Apart from a largely photographic German-language publication released by edel Verlag in 1992, and Paul Hickey’s 2011 memoir Sometimes – A Life of Love, Loss & Erasure, there have been few book-length accounts connected with the band. Neither, however, offers a comprehensive history of Erasure told from the perspective of its fans.

Now, with All Through the Years: A Fan’s History of Erasure, 1985–2026, longtime fan Ewan McLaren has set out to fill that gap. Bringing together four decades of research, personal memories and first-hand experiences, his book explores not only the band’s history but also the friendships, encounters and shared experiences that have grown around its music.

As someone who has followed Erasure for decades and written about the band as an online music journalist, I was particularly interested when news of the book first emerged. I soon got in touch with Ewan, and it quickly became clear that we shared more than just a passion for the same band. There was also a mutual curiosity and appreciation for each other’s experiences.

That gave us the idea of a conversation that goes beyond a conventional book interview. We wanted to explore two different perspectives on being an Erasure fan: Ewan’s experiences growing up in the UK and my own memories of following the band in Hungary. There are plenty of similarities, but also some striking differences shaped by geography, culture and the very different opportunities available to fans on either side of Europe.

This is a conversation about music, memories, friendships, fan communities and the unexpected ways in which a band can become part of someone’s life – sometimes for more than forty years.

Ewan McLaren interview on Erasure

From the first encounter to a lifelong passion

SL: Everyone has their own story of discovering a band that eventually becomes an important part of their life. My own Erasure story began in a rather unexpected way. The first time I encountered Oh L’Amour was actually through Dollar’s version, which I heard in a cinema before a film screening. Later, I came across Sometimes on the radio, but I wouldn’t say I was a fan just yet. That really began around 1989, when I started high school. How did your own Erasure story begin? Was it love at first listen?

Ewan: I remember seeing Sometimes for the first time – probably on Top of the Pops, probably around the time of my 15th birthday. I liked it straight away, but at that point it was nothing more than that. I registered It Doesn’t Have to Be similarly, and this continued through Victim of Love, where I admit I had a bit of a wobble.

Times at school weren’t the easiest for me, and I remember Andy appearing on British TV in a black rubber leotard. If I’d admitted I was a fan at that point, it would have given certain groups at school more ammunition to throw at me, as unfortunately there was a large homophobic element amongst my peers.

However, when The Circus single was released, that was the final straw. I was hooked, and I had to find out as much as I could about the band. I was prepared to live with any consequences that came my way.

The first records and the collecting obsession

SL: My first Erasure CD was Two Ring Circus, although I bought it several years after its original release. As a teenager, and later as a university student with a fairly limited budget, cassette copying was still an important part of how we shared and discovered music. Do you remember the first Erasure record you bought? Did collecting the band’s releases become an important part of your fandom?

Ewan: My timing was fortunate in some respects, because it was The Circus single that pushed me to actually start buying records. I began by buying the 12-inch singles for that release. Each contained a number of live tracks, so by purchasing all three, I was able to experience quite a bit of the existing catalogue. That was where the love affair began.

After that, collecting became a passion of mine. I started off by attempting to buy every format and edition so that I could make sure I’d heard every commercially available track or remix. Over time, this expanded to whatever I could lay my hands on, and I did build up quite a collection!

The first time live

SL: My first Erasure concert was in 1992, at Budapest’s Kisstadion, during the legendary Phantasmagorical Entertainment tour. I even took a tape recorder with me, hoping to capture the show – although, looking back, the recording contains more of the audience, including my own voice, than the actual band! What was your first Erasure concert like?

Ewan: Glasgow SECC, December 1989. A local record shop ran coaches to concerts from my home town, so a friend and I went. It was the first time I’d ever been to a concert, and I really wasn’t sure what to expect. A two-hour coach journey each way in Scotland in December, pitch black all the way.

As I recall, the setlist for that tour started off quite slowly, opening with Piano Song and How Many Times?. I stood there, taking it all in, but up to that point I wasn’t really seeing what the big attraction was. The audience was fairly quiet too.

However, when Chains of Love started, the audience seemed to explode and the energy was infectious. That was the moment when it all made sense, and when watching the band perform live became something I wanted to do again and again.

Live performance is a special feeling for me. Being in a crowd of people and feeding off their energy when they hear a track they know and love really is amazing.

In short, I love the music because it can be listened to in isolation, and songs can have a very unique meaning to different people. But seeing the band live is an opportunity to share that love.

Finding other fans: fanzines, fan clubs and photocopies

SL: I discovered the existence of a small Erasure fan club at Budapest’s Petőfi Csarnok relatively late, and I first visited it in 1994. I remember bringing along a videotape containing an episode of the German VIVA TV programme Jam featuring Erasure, which I could share with other fans.

The club also produced a small photocopied fanzine called Mánia, largely based on translated excerpts from Private Ear, but supplemented with Hungarian news and local developments. I even sent them a caricature of Erasure that I’d drawn spontaneously, and they used it as the cover of one of their issues.

How did the Erasure fan community develop in the UK? Was the official fan club and Private Ear the main way of connecting with other fans?

Ewan: Before the internet, the official fan club and Private Ear were really the only ways I knew of to connect with other fans. If there were local groups, I wasn’t aware of them at the time.

Once email and mailing lists arrived in the mid-90s, things opened up a lot. There was the Wonderland mailing list, and independent fanzines like The Erasure Files, which is how I ended up producing my own.

It sounds a bit like what you describe with Mánia. Fans everywhere seem to have found their own ways of making a small community out of photocopies and enthusiasm.

Different countries, different experiences – the same passion

SL: Growing up as an Erasure fan in Hungary during the late 1980s and early 1990s was quite different from being a fan in the UK. Access to records, information and concerts was often much more limited, and fans had to find their own ways of building communities and sharing their enthusiasm.

Do you think being an Erasure fan in the UK was fundamentally different from being a fan in countries such as Hungary or other parts of Eastern Europe? Did you ever have a sense that the band’s music could mean something particularly powerful to fans in places where access to the band and its world was much more limited?

Ewan: I can only answer that from the outside, because I haven’t lived it. I guess UK fans have been very fortunate over the years compared with other countries. The band were on Top of the Pops, in the record shops and touring regularly, so access was never really the problem. The challenge was finding other fans.

What I do know from researching the book is how much it meant for the band to play in places like that. Daniel Miller’s favourite Erasure show was Prague in November 1989, three days after the Berlin Wall fell, and by 1992 they were taking the tour to Budapest as well.

As for whether the music could mean something particularly powerful to fans in places with more limited access, it’s probably not something I thought about during the band’s commercial peak. But I’d like to think that good music works anywhere in the world. Reading about your experience, it sounds as though fans there had to be far more inventive than we ever did.

When music leads to lifelong friendships

SL: Some of the friendships I made through the fan club became much stronger around the time of Erasure’s 1997 Budapest concert. Looking back, the music was really just the starting point for friendships and shared experiences that continued beyond the band itself. Did you make lasting friendships through the Erasure fan community? And do you think these friendships were among the most important things that grew out of being a fan?

Ewan: Undoubtedly, and it sounds like Budapest did the same for you.

Whenever Erasure tour, part of the planning before shows is working out who else we know is going to the same show or shows, and making plans to meet up beforehand.

Similarly, when Erasure did the four anniversary shows in the UK last year, there were so many people there who I’m still close friends with, or who I simply hadn’t seen in years. We hung around in the venue after the show chatting until the venue staff had to quietly ask us to leave!

From fan to active participant

SL: At some point, being a fan can become something more than simply listening to music or attending concerts. You begin to contribute to the community, share information, create things, organise activities or help others discover the band. When did you first feel the urge to become actively involved in the Erasure world?

Ewan: A small correction first: I’ve been an EIS member for many years and have helped out where I could, but I’ve never been part of the team that runs it.

Through the early 90s, I had a feeling that my affection for the band was such that I’d like to be more involved, but each time an opportunity came along, it fell into my lap rather than being something I went looking for.

My own involvement really began in 1996, when I started helping promote another fan’s fanzine, and then launched my own when he stopped. That led to fan gatherings and eventually to helping Greg and Alan organise the official EIS’04 convention.

SL: Was there ever a moment when you realised that the work you were doing was genuinely important to other fans?

Ewan: I don’t think I ever had one of those moments, to be honest. I’ve done what I can whenever the opportunity has arisen, and the nicest part has been seeing other fans enjoy things such as EIS’04.

But I still don’t consider myself as anything other than a fan. A very fortunate one!

Personal connections with Vince and Andy

SL: In 1994, a few members of the Hungarian fan club had the opportunity to meet Erasure during their visit to Hungary in connection with the Goldene Europa award. Some footage of that meeting even appears briefly in the acoustic video for Sono Luminus.

My own first personal meeting with Vince and Andy came in 2005, when I interviewed them in Munich before their concert. Since then, I’ve had the opportunity to see Erasure live several more times – in Munich in 2007, Budapest in 2011, Vienna in 2017 and Munich again in 2018. On each of those occasions, we met backstage, and over the years the relationship became increasingly personal. During the more recent encounters, Vince and Andy greeted me like a friend, and they’d even got to know my family.

How did your own relationship with Vince and Andy develop over the years? Did you ever experience a similar evolution, from being a fan who followed the band closely to becoming a familiar face and eventually someone they knew personally?

Ewan: The first time I met Vince and Andy was in 1997 at the Cowboy concerts, at the stage door in Sheffield. I genuinely thought at the time that was it. I’d met them, said thank you for the music, and it wouldn’t happen again.

I certainly didn’t expect to have the good fortune to meet them, or spend time with them, as many times as I have. The next time was the aftershow party after the London show in 2003, and the year after, Andy surprised everyone by turning up at EIS’04.

That’s a really good question, and in some respects a tough one! I’ve never really considered that I have a relationship as such with the band. But when we saw Andy after one of his solo shows last year, he was so pleased to see my wife, and that was a lovely moment to see. It meant more to me than any recognition I may have got from Andy myself.

SL: And beyond Vince and Andy, how important were your relationships with the people behind the scenes – the fan club organisers, for example?

Ewan: Very important, but mostly on the fan club side. Janet, Jonny, Greg and later Richard were the people who made so much of this possible, whether that was a mention in Private Ear, a tip about where to wait after a show, or being asked to help put on EIS’04.

Greg and I became friends after he gave us passes to an aftershow, and he ended up being my best man.

I’ve never really had a relationship with the label or the production side, other than a few backstage conversations along the way, so I’d be wary of claiming one. But the people who’ve run the fan club over the years have all clearly cared about the band and the fans, and I’ve been lucky to know all of them, in varying capacities.

The most memorable Erasure moment – and a love story

SL: After more than four decades of following Erasure, there must be countless memories, concerts, encounters and unexpected moments that have stayed with you. Is there one particular Erasure-related experience that stands out above all the others as the most meaningful part of your journey with the band?

Ewan: There really are so many instances I could choose here, but it would be remiss of me – and probably not the best decision for my marriage, lol – if I didn’t say that it was meeting a young lady called Donna at the All Through the Years Erasure convention and party in Nottingham in 1998.

Donna became my wife, and we were married on the morning of EIS’04 in Leicester. Without the band, we would never have met, and we’re still happily married – and both still fans, of course – to this day.

The internet and the changing nature of fandom

SL: The way fans connect with each other has changed enormously over the past four decades. From fanzines, newsletters, letters and cassette recordings to websites, forums and social media, the possibilities of sharing information and experiences have become almost limitless.

How do you think the internet fundamentally changed the experience of being an Erasure fan? Did it bring fans closer together, or do you think something also disappeared from the more personal, slower-moving fan culture of the pre-internet era?

Ewan: For me personally, the internet changed things in a positive way, and the only thing I probably lost was my sense of isolation as an Erasure fan.

Prior to this, my Erasure news came either from music magazines or from Private Ear. In terms of contact with other fans, there really wasn’t any – other than a pen pal I had via the EIS.

Once I had internet access, I stumbled across the Wonderland mailing list, which is where I first met many people who I’m still good friends with today.

At that point, news from the band became more instant, as the EIS moved from print to website and email, which vastly sped up the flow of information from band to fan.

The next chapter – the excitement never goes away

SL: As a longtime fan, I’m sure the anticipation of new Erasure music and another tour never completely disappears. With a new album and tour on the horizon, how are you feeling about this next chapter? Does the excitement of waiting for new music and seeing the band live still feel the same as it did in the early years?

Ewan: That excitement still remains. When Richard announced in the newsletter that we should tune into BBC Radio 2 the following Monday for some special Erasure announcements, the excitement in our house was off the scale.

All weekend we were literally saying, “Is it not Monday yet?” and counting down the hours.

Once the tour dates were announced, we spent some time looking through the venue list to work out an itinerary of which shows we could feasibly attend. And then came the stress on presale morning, trying to ensure we got the best seats we could for each chosen show.

Hearing Wings of Love for the first time was another special moment. On that first listen, I had tears in my eyes…

All Through the Years – how the book came to life

SL: At what point did you realise that your own experiences and the history of the Erasure fan community could become a book? Was this something you’d been thinking about for years, or did the idea gradually take shape?

Ewan: During the COVID lockdowns, I started collating all the bits and pieces I had regarding the band into some semblance of order and began taking notes. As the years progressed, I would return to it semi-regularly and start fleshing it out. I could see it was beginning to become more of a story.

What pushed me on was my own frustration that there wasn’t anything similar available, as I would have loved to have read it myself. And when I did find something, it inevitably annoyed me when it was missing what I would consider key details.

SL: Was there anything you discovered during your research that genuinely surprised you or changed the way you looked at a particular period in the band’s history?

Ewan: I wouldn’t say that anything I discovered changed my opinion of the band or any particular era, but I did find some facts I wasn’t previously aware of.

Whilst not directly related to Erasure themselves, I discovered that Val Chalmers, Erasure’s longtime backing vocalist alongside her sister Emma, had recorded backing vocals for Dave Stewart and The Spiritual Cowboys in the early 1990s. It was on an album that didn’t receive much mainstream attention, but one that I’ve owned and loved for over 35 years.

Who is the book for?

SL: Who do you primarily see as the audience for All Through the Years? Is it mainly intended for longtime fans who lived through the band’s history, or do you also hope to reach younger readers who may have discovered Erasure more recently?

Ewan: The main audience is the fanbase: people who lived through it, who’ll recognise the tours, the newsletters and the conventions.

But I’ve tried to fill the book with real-life stories, such as queueing for tickets, travelling to shows and friendships made through a band – things that any longtime fan of any band would recognise.

As for younger readers, I’d love that. Erasure keep finding new listeners, and a chapter like the one on A Little Respect shows how a song keeps reaching people who never knew the band. I hope the book can be a way in for them as well.

SL: Who was the first person you showed the manuscript to, and was there anyone whose feedback particularly influenced the final version?

Ewan: Other than my wife, who is obviously biased, I sent the draft to a small number of trusted friends, each chosen for something different.

Barbara, an Erasure fan I’ve known for over twenty years and whose daughter I’m godparent to, was the first to read it. I knew her feedback would be honest, and she’s excellent at judging the feeling of a text. She loved it!

Peter is the one most likely to catch any factual slips regarding releases, such as catalogue numbers and track listings.

And Tina, who is only a casual fan, was perfect for reading it from a completely different perspective.

Each of them gave feedback that helped the book become what it is today. I’m very grateful to all three.

More than the music – a lifetime lived alongside it

SL: The back cover of the book contains a line that I particularly like:

“More than the music. A lifetime lived alongside it.”

After spending so many years researching, collecting memories and writing about Erasure, what does the publication of the book mean to you personally? Is there a sense of finally putting something into perspective, or does it feel more like the beginning of another chapter in your own Erasure journey?

Ewan: Over the past few years, I’ve realised that I know a number of things about the band’s history that aren’t widely known, and it would be a shame if those memories were lost.

A particular reason for doing so is that my son is in his mid-twenties now and has had to grow up with two Erasure fans as his parents. But he doesn’t know – or in some cases remember – half of the wonderful things that loving this band has brought us.

I’d like to think that one day in the future, when I’m no longer around to tell these stories, he could reach for a copy on his own bookshelf, and my voice would live on in his head.

I’ve thoroughly enjoyed the process, and I would really like to write some more, but the difficulty would be finding a subject that I have the same passion for and knowledge of.

SL: And finally, if someone who knew nothing about Erasure picked up your book, what would you most hope they would take away from it?

Ewan: I’d hope they’d come away understanding the warmth and affection that exists between the fans and the band, and just as much among the fans themselves.

More than forty years later

What becomes particularly clear from this conversation is that the story of Erasure is about much more than albums, singles, tours and chart positions. It is also a story about people who found each other through music, formed friendships and created memories that have lasted for decades.

Ewan’s experiences in the UK and my own memories of the Hungarian fan community show just how different the circumstances could be for fans in different parts of Europe – and yet how similar the passion remained.

While access to records, concerts and information was relatively straightforward in the UK, fans in Hungary often had to improvise, build their own networks and find creative ways to share their enthusiasm. Small fan clubs, photocopied fanzines, exchanged recordings and personal friendships became an essential part of that experience.

Perhaps that is what makes All Through the Years particularly valuable. It doesn’t simply preserve the history of a band; it also captures the story of a community and the people whose lives have been shaped by their shared love of music.

And sometimes, as Ewan’s story so beautifully illustrates, that shared passion can lead to something even more meaningful – a lifelong friendship, a marriage, or memories that become part of a family’s history.

As the book’s subtitle reminds us, it is about much more than the music. It is about a lifetime lived alongside it.

Further information about All Through the Years: A Fan’s History of Erasure, 1985–2026 can be found on the official website: www.erasurebook.com

About Erasure

Erasure are the English synth-pop duo of vocalist Andy Bell and instrumentalist Vince Clarke, formed in London in 1985. Clarke had already co-founded Depeche Mode, formed Yazoo with Alison Moyet and led the short-lived trio The Assembly before pairing with Bell. The duo signed to Mute Records and released their debut album, “Wonderland,” in 1986, followed by a run of hits including “Sometimes,” “A Little Respect,” “Chains of Love,” “Blue Savannah” and “Always.” Erasure have won a BRIT Award and an Ivor Novello Award, and marked 40 years of “Who Needs Love Like That” in September 2025.

The duo’s most recent studio album together was “Day-Glo (Based on a True Story),” released in August 2022. Erasure announced a new album, “Radio!! Radio!!,” alongside the single “Wings of Love” and a 2027 tour in September 2026, and followed it with a Ladytron remix of “Wings Of Love” and a CD single in November 2026. “Radio!! Radio!!” is due on Mute on March 12, 2027.

Ewan McLaren’s book, “All Through the Years: A Fan’s History of Erasure, 1985-2026,” is an independent, unofficial history of the band told through four decades of fan memory, research and first-hand experience. It is available through the book’s official website, www.erasurebook.com.

items.title: Sabotage Q.C.Q.C.? announce ‘Gone’ and three more digital reissues
items.summary: Front 242, Pankow, Die Warzau and Meathead – some familiar names appear in the latest...
items.fullText:
Front 242, Pankow, Die Warzau and Meathead – some familiar names appear in the latest batch of digital reissues announced by German EBM and electro-punk outfit Sabotage Q.C.Q.C.? Alongside three releases from their 1990s catalogue, the band have announced the four-track release “Gone” for December 20, 2026.

‘Schlager’ (1997)

Originally released as a CD single in 1997, “Schlager” became digitally available on November 26 through Norway’s Sub Culture Records.

Recorded at Art & Strategy Studios and produced by Front 242’s Daniel Bressanutti and Patrick Codenys, the release features the title track and two versions of “Heidenangst”, including a Pankow remix.

Interestingly, the production of “Schlager” also laid the foundations for NUDE, a separate project originally comprising Isabelle Gernand, Daniel Bressanutti and Marc Werner.

‘Tumulte’ (1993)

On November 27, Sub Culture Records will digitally reissue the band’s debut album “Tumulte”.

According to the band, a joint tour through Germany was followed by production sessions in Florence, Italy, with Paolo Favati, Maurizio Fasolo and Federico Panero.

Originally released through Danse Macabre, the label associated with German darkwave pioneers Das Ich, the album included the club hit “Les Fleurs du Mal” as well as “En Ordre” and “Ewigkeit”.

More than 30 years later, both songs are part of the band’s current release schedule. Several new versions of “En Ordre” appeared on November 14, while a reworked “Ewigkeit” is due in January.

‘Acoustic Costumes’ (1998)

The next digital reissue through Sub Culture Records follows on December 18. Originally released on the British label Nightbreed Recordings, “Acoustic Costumes” contains rare remixes and alternative recordings.

Front 242’s Daniel Bressanutti and Patrick Codenys contributed production work to “Goddess” and “Nau-Sea”, with Bressanutti also remixing “Wild Child”. Further contributions include Pankow’s versions of “Do What You Do” and “Escape”, Die Warzau’s remixes of “Hearts & Bombs” and “Freiheit”, and Meathead’s interpretation of “DWYD (Reprise)”.

‘Gone’ (2026)

Just two days later, on December 20, Sabotage will release “Gone”. The band describe the song as a dancefloor-oriented composition with driving basslines and forceful rhythms.

Three versions of the title track are included: the “Hold Tight Mix”, “Hold On Mix” and “Beside Me Mix”, accompanied by “The Flood (Tumulte Version)”. An earlier alternative version, the “Riot Mix”, appeared on the recent “En Ordre” release.

“The Flood” will also feature on the limited 12-inch vinyl EP “No Bottom – No Top”, due January 15, 2027, through Germany’s Emmo.biz Records. The EP additionally includes “Impuls Kontakt”, “Souvenir (Rework)” and “Ewigkeit (Reprise)”.

A completely new studio album is planned for 2027.

Sabotage Q.C.Q.C.? release schedule

  • November 26, 2026: “Schlager” (digital reissue, Sub Culture Records)
  • November 27, 2026: “Tumulte” (digital reissue, Sub Culture Records)
  • December 18, 2026: “Acoustic Costumes” (digital reissue, Sub Culture Records)
  • December 20, 2026: “Gone” (digital release)
  • January 15, 2027: “No Bottom – No Top” (limited 12-inch vinyl EP, Emmo.biz Records)
  • 2027: New studio album (planned)

About Sabotage Q.C.Q.C.?

Sabotage Q.C.Q.C.? is a German EBM and electro-punk act whose current lineup includes Isabelle Gernand, Marc Werner, Detlef Weinreich and Johannes Buchner. The band’s recorded history goes back more than three decades, starting with the 1993 album “Tumulte,” followed by “Annorlunda” (1994), “Les Enfants Sauvages” (1995), “Schlager” (1997) and “Acoustic Costumes” (1998).

Those five 1990s releases are being reissued digitally through Sub Culture Records, a label run by longtime band associate Per Aksel Lundgreen, with “Annorlunda” and “Les Enfants Sauvages” out since November 13, 2026 and “Schlager,” “Tumulte” and “Acoustic Costumes” following through November and December. The band is also preparing new material: the single “Gone” on December 20, 2026, and a limited 12-inch vinyl EP, “No Bottom – No Top,” through Germany’s Emmo.biz Records on January 15, 2027, ahead of a full-length studio album planned for later in 2027.

items.title: Andy Taylor, Duran Duran guitarist, dies aged 65
items.summary: Andy Taylor, guitarist with Duran Duran from 1980 to 1985 and 2001 to 2006, has died aged 65, after a prostate cancer diagnosis revealed in 2022.
items.fullText:
Andy Taylor, the guitarist who played on Duran Duran’s run of 1980s hits, died on 23 November 2026 at the age of 65, his bandmates announced in a joint statement. The statement, signed by Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor, cited “a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer.” Side-Line reported in November 2022 that Taylor had revealed a stage four diagnosis in a letter read out at Duran Duran’s induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

The bandmates’ statement traced Taylor’s role in the group back to its earliest days: “Andy was there at the very beginning of our story. […] From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. […] His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed. […] Our thoughts are with his wife Tracey, his children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and grandson Albie. They all loved him deeply and we ask that their privacy be respected at this very difficult time.”

Taylor’s wife, Tracey, described him as “the rock of our family” and said “we will miss him every single day.” She added: “For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. […] Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home.” Of his illness, she said: “Andy faced the last few years with so much courage and determination. He never gave up, fighting until the very end, never losing his love of life. […] The kindness and support shown to him by fans from all over the world throughout his illness brought him immense comfort and strength, and for that we will always be grateful.”

Simon Le Bon also issued a personal statement: “Andy never took the easy musical route. […] His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later. […] There’s a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart. It’ll never close up; I won’t let it. I will miss him & love him for all my days.” Rod Stewart, who worked with Taylor in the late 1980s, called him his “dear pal” on Instagram, writing: “We made some good music together and at the same time had some outrageous fun.”

Taylor’s death comes eleven days after bandmate Roger Taylor announced he was stepping down as Duran Duran’s drummer, citing a worsening tinnitus diagnosis.

Andy Taylor’s career with Duran Duran

Andrew James Taylor was born on 16 February 1961 in Tynemouth, Northumberland, and raised in nearby Cullercoats, the son of a fisherman. Self-taught on guitar, bass and drums, he was playing professionally by the age of 13. He answered an advertisement in a music paper seeking a “live-wire guitarist” and travelled by train to Birmingham to audition, joining Duran Duran in April 1980; the band signed to EMI that December.

Taylor co-wrote and played guitar on Duran Duran hits including “Girls on Film,” “Hungry Like the Wolf,” “Save a Prayer” and “Rio.” He left the band in 1985, following its performance at Live Aid that July. In his 2008 autobiography, “Wild Boy: My Life in Duran Duran,” he recalled the mood on the way to the show: “We’d reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other. […] We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral.” The remaining trio of Le Bon, Rhodes and John Taylor went on to record the 1986 album “Notorious” with producer Nile Rodgers, without Taylor or Roger Taylor.

During Duran Duran’s 1985 hiatus, Taylor and bassist John Taylor had already formed the Power Station with singer Robert Palmer and session drummer Tony Thompson. The group’s self-titled album reached the top 20 in the UK and the top 10 in the US, led by the singles “Some Like It Hot” and “Get It On (Bang a Gong).” Taylor also played lead guitar on Palmer’s “Addicted to Love,” from his 1985 album “Riptide.” Taylor released his debut solo album, “Thunder,” in 1987, and between 1987 and 1988 co-wrote and co-produced Rod Stewart’s album “Out of Order,” contributing to the singles “Lost in You,” “Forever Young” and “My Heart Can’t Tell You No.” He also played lead guitar on “Mad About You,” from Belinda Carlisle’s 1986 album “Belinda.”

Taylor rejoined Duran Duran in 2001 and played on the album “Astronaut” (2004) and its single “(Reach Up for The) Sunrise,” before leaving the band again in 2006 during the recording of what became “Red Carpet Massacre” (2007). He did not attend Duran Duran’s induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022; Le Bon read out a letter in which Taylor revealed he had been diagnosed with stage four prostate cancer in 2018. Taylor returned to contribute to Duran Duran’s most recent album, “Danse Macabre” (2023), his final work with the band.

About Andy Taylor

items.title: Onasander & RNGMNN – Illumination Phases (Digital/CD Album – Winter-Light)
items.summary: Both Maurizio Landini (Onasander) and Ronny Engmann (Rngmnn) are no strangers to collaboration. Although both...
items.fullText:
Both Maurizio Landini (Onasander) and Ronny Engmann (Rngmnn) are no strangers to collaboration. Although both artists primarily work with others, they occasionally venture out on their own. This album brings together two perspectives in a hushed exploration of borderlands—places where boundaries blur and new worlds emerge.

This concept forms the foundation for eight tracks. The listener is transported into an alien universe, drifting across an imaginary, dark sea of low-frequency, vibrating sound waves. The droning tones may initially seem monotonous, but they are constructed with great care and, above all, patience. Occasionally, additional sounds emerge, creating subtle yet striking effects. The atmosphere is grim, at times even ominous, enhanced by minute sonic details that seem to foreshadow an impending ordeal or tragedy. The final track gradually builds to a crescendo, leaving the listener with a lingering sense of discomfort and dread.

Occupying a space somewhere between Dark-Ambient and, predominantly, Cinematic music, this is a deeply affecting release. An excellent collaboration that fully lives up to the high standards I have come to expect from Onasander. (Rating:8).

Listen to “In The Twilight Of The Last Quarter”:

About Onasander & RNGMNN

Onasander is the dark ambient and cinematic project of Italian musician Maurizio Landini. Landini has released prolifically through collaborations with artists including Kloob, Ajna, Alphaxone, Ashtoreth and Nimh, mostly through the Winter-Light label, and issued his first true solo album, “Dawn Metrics”, in 2024.

RNGMNN is the solo dark ambient project of German artist Ronny Engmann. The project has released several albums through Winter-Light, including “False Dawn” in 2021 and “Never Sleep Again” with Karina Dorin in 2024. “Illumination Phases” is the pair’s first joint album together.

items.title: Brood Faye Hauls a Sailor’s Ghost Ashore in Video for Sordid Shanty “Sea Song” — “Hypnotist” EP Announced!
items.summary: A salty apparition Ran o’er with salt and grime Thought he could get his way with me And get away with crime A bad dream can leave you awake at… The post Brood Faye Hauls a Sailor’s Ghost Ashore in Video for Sordid Shanty “Sea Song” — “Hypnotist” EP Announced!
items.fullText:
A salty apparition

Ran o’er with salt and grime

Thought he could get his way with me

And get away with crime

A bad dream can leave you awake at four in the morning, trying to put words to things that made a terrible kind of sense while you were asleep. You can get every detail right and still have trouble asking the person beside you to stay awake a little longer. Zach Webber, the vocalist and driving force behind Brood Faye, brings that unease to Hypnotist, an EP preoccupied with what happens when somebody, or something, is listening. On the opening track, “Sea Song,” that listener is close enough to reach for in the dark.

The trouble begins with an oil-soaked lamp, the one thing the man in the song likes among a woman’s possessions. The drowned sailor who owned it turns up in a dream, crusted with salt and grime, and tries to force himself on the dreamer. Webber is just as particular about what follows, down to the damp mattress and the way the man’s partner holds his hand and rubs his neck. She has a sharp word for his pride, too, which makes “as long as I’ve got you” sound like the kind of reassurance only someone who knows him well could give.

Drums ring out through reverb before the EBM beat settles in. Webber recites the first lines through layers of effects with the cool detachment of someone describing a secondhand purchase. A high synth melody draws out a softer performance, and the weight of the Oberheim TEO-5 bass under those gauzy tones recalls the ’90s dance records that found room for shoegaze and dream pop on the club floor.

Surf rolls over dark sand before Pete Magine cuts to a figure walking through a fluorescent-lit passage. Magine directed and shot the video from a concept he developed with Webber, who appears alongside co-star Mimi Chakravorty. When one camera began turning the brightest parts of the frame black, they layered that footage with shots from a second camera. Faces overlap and break into horizontal bands. The eye gets a moment’s rest when Webber and Chakravorty lean back to back in the dark.

On the song and the video, Zach Webber explains:

“Sea Song was originally called Dr. Jones. For some reason Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom was in my head, and while it may have mildly inspired the theme of the lyrics it otherwise did not have any function, so I changed it to fit the context of the story. Unfortunately Academy Award Winner Ke Huy Quan was not available for the video (haha), so we got Mimi, who was a shoo-in for the job as our androgynous Art Deco Tawny Kitane. My good friend Pete Magine directed, shot, and co-conceived the video with me, drawing from 90s MTV in the vein of Duran Duran, The Prodigy, and Michael Bolton. Dramatic movements, low tech. Pete’s first camera started hyperventilating and etching all the lightest cells in the image pitch black, which we obviously felt was too cool to lose and fit the story. Then we layered shots from the other camera on top, blending the two dimensions.

Lyrically, crafting a story was important to me when I started writing. I wanted to repair what I perceived as an overall lack in all my previous songs: not enough specificity. This is funny, because I write gratuitously compared to my peers. I’ve never been one for honing to the finite. I swung hard with this one though, to the point which these lyrics are arguably too specific. But I do think in the confusing onslaught of story someone might find universality they can connect with. It’s a really fucked up story about a guy, me probably, having a dream about a ghoulish sailor ghost trying to fuck me, waking up sweating and being comforted by my partner. That’s kinda it. It doesn’t make any sense to me as to why I wrote it, I have no precise foundation for this except maybe that I’ve experienced a lot of sexual assault and aggression against me, mostly from men, and wanted partners who sympathized with me concurrently, which I never received. Maybe writing and performing this was a fantasy I needed to play out. Maybe.

Unabashedly, I just want to be dark electro Michael Hutchence. I’m not ashamed to admit it. In my previous work, I was doing a lot of Ohgr-style vocalizing and was afraid to sing or sound pretty, so I tried to let go of that for this song. While it’s content is bizarre and gross, I wanted the sound to be sexy for contrast. Unabashedly again, I have made stringent use of my relatively new Oberheim TEO-5, trying out new patches of my own, but the bass on this song is the ElctroBdyBass preset. I think Oberheim might be tapped into what we’ve got goin’ on in the scene, because I was shocked when I saw it was called that. From here on out I’ll be building my own patches for bass, but I wanted to make explicit inaugural use of the preset first, and make it known… unabashedly.”

Brood Faye’s Hypnotist is out December 4, 2026, via Wie Ein Gott Records. Webber produced and recorded the EP and mixed it with Chad Gordon, who also mastered it. Chris Campion created the cover artwork.

items.title: David Carretta and Back From The Wave share ‘Fleshpots’
items.summary: David Carretta and Back From The Wave share "Fleshpots", a new single out November 25, 2026 via Iptamenos Discos, Local Suicide's Berlin imprint.
items.fullText:
French electroclash pioneer David Carretta and fellow French producer Back From The Wave have released “Fleshpots”, a new single out November 25, 2026 via Iptamenos Discos, Local Suicide’s Berlin-based imprint.

The track pairs Carretta’s punk and new wave-rooted club sound with Back From The Wave’s EBM and New Beat leanings, built around a percussive analogue synth line and vocals delivered with a punk rocker’s bravado. Its repeated refrain, “Switch off the light / Switch on your pleasure,” runs through the track as its recurring hook.

“Fleshpots” is the second release to bring the two artists together on Iptamenos Discos: Back From The Wave previously released “Love Is Not Enough” with Idoru on the label, and his music has also appeared on Carretta’s own Space Factory label, which issued his “Psychic” EP, later remixed by Carretta. “Fleshpots” is out now via Iptamenos Discos and available on Spotify and other digital and streaming platforms.

About David Carretta and Back From The Wave

David Carretta has worked in the French electronic underground since the late 1990s, carrying the raw spirit of his punk and new wave beginnings into club music. His early releases appeared on Harthouse and International Deejay Gigolo, followed by albums including “Le Catalogue Electronique” and “Kill Your Radio.” His single “Vicious Game” helped establish him within the electroclash movement of the 2000s, alongside The Hacker, Miss Kittin and Vitalic. Side-Line spoke with Carretta for a “Click Interview” in 2016. He also runs the label Space Factory, which has released music from Jostronamer, Victoria Lukas and Back From The Wave, whose 2023 “Psychic” EP Carretta later remixed.

Back From The Wave is the project of French producer Fred Rodrigues Carreira, who has made music since the late 1990s and has released under his current name since 2019, moving between electro, EBM, New Beat and indie dance. His catalogue includes releases on Bordello A Parigi, Melodize and Ritmo Fatale, and his tracks have been played by DJs including DJ Hell, Jennifer Cardini, The Hacker and Kendal. He returned to Iptamenos Discos on “Love Is Not Enough” with Idoru, released in June 2026, before teaming up with Carretta on “Fleshpots.”

items.title: Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Has Passed Away at 65
items.summary: Andy Taylor, the guitarist and co-writer who gave Duran Duran’s early records their bite, died on Monday, November 23, at 65. His family and former bandmates announced on Wednesday that… The post Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Has Passed Away at 65 appeared
items.fullText:
Andy Taylor, the guitarist and co-writer who gave Duran Duran’s early records their bite, died on Monday, November 23, at 65. His family and former bandmates announced on Wednesday that he died at home with his family beside him after a long illness with prostate cancer.

Taylor’s wife, Tracey, remembered a husband, father and grandfather who was happiest when the family was together. She said, “For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first.” She recalled his determination to keep enjoying life through his illness and thanked fans for the comfort their support brought him. The family took comfort in knowing he felt loved.

Simon Le Bon, John Taylor, Nick Rhodes and Roger Taylor recalled the confidence Taylor brought with him to Birmingham and the dry humor that kept them grounded as the band took off. “His playing drove the songs that took us around the world,” they wrote. They said getting to play together again in the early 2000s meant a great deal to them. His letter at the 2022 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction reminded them how close they still were.

Read the full statement and the band members’ individual tributes here.

Born February 16, 1961, Taylor grew up in Cullercoats on England’s northeast coast. He played working men’s clubs around Newcastle in his teens and had already toured Europe by the time he answered Duran Duran’s Melody Maker ad in 1980. He moved to Birmingham, and that July the classic five-piece played its first gig together at the Rum Runner, the nightclub where they rehearsed.

Taylor co-wrote and played on 1981’s Duran Duran, 1982’s Rio and 1983’s Seven and the Ragged Tiger. His clipped chords on “Girls on Film” leave John Taylor’s bass room to dart around them. “Careless Memories” has the impatient scrape of a band still within earshot of punk. On “Hungry Like the Wolf,” Taylor’s riff is as easy to hum as the chorus.

Andy and John Taylor formed the Power Station with singer Robert Palmer and Chic drummer Tony Thompson. On their 1985 debut, Andy’s heavy guitar chords and Thompson’s outsized drums drove “Some Like It Hot” and a cover of T. Rex’s “Get It On.” Taylor played with both bands at Live Aid in Philadelphia that July. He left Duran Duran in 1986 and released his solo debut, Thunder, the following year. He also played on Palmer’s “Addicted to Love” and co-produced Rod Stewart’s Out of Order.

The classic Duran Duran lineup reunited in 2001 and returned to the stage in 2003. They released Astronaut in 2004, their first studio album together since Seven and the Ragged Tiger. Taylor left again in 2006.

When Duran Duran entered the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, illness kept Taylor from the ceremony. Le Bon read from Taylor’s letter disclosing his diagnosis of stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer. The following year, Taylor played alongside Nile Rodgers on “Black Moonlight,” from Duran Duran’s Danse Macabre, and released a solo album, Man’s a Wolf to Man.

Taylor is survived by his wife, Tracey, their children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and his grandson Albie. His former bandmates asked people to respect the family’s privacy. In lieu of flowers, the family has asked for donations in his memory to Prostate Cancer UK.
