“The God Particle” is available as a digital album on Bandcamp.

About Unify Separate

Unify Separate is the Scottish-Swedish electronic duo of Andrew Montgomery and Leo Josefsson, formed in Stockholm in 2015 and initially performing under the name US. Montgomery previously fronted British alternative band Geneva, which released music through Nude Records during the 1990s. Josefsson’s earlier credits include Statemachine and LOWE, both recognised at the Scandinavian Alternative Music Awards; he also co-produced Priest’s 2026 album “Altered State Police” with Linton Rubino, has worked with Rednex and Nassim Al Fakir, and has directed visual work for Diary of Dreams and The Mobile Homes, operating out of his Kiss the Needle studio in Stockholm.

Unify Separate released their debut album, “First Contact,” in 2019, followed by “Music Since Tomorrow,” issued digitally in 2022 and reissued on CD in 2023 with contributions from Suede guitarist Richard Oakes on “The Void” and “Waiting Game.” Touring with Diary of Dreams across Germany, Sweden and the United Kingdom fed into the harder electronic direction first heard on the duo’s 2025 “Heavy Meta” material, a progression that continues on “The God Particle.” Josefsson discussed the album’s themes and the duo’s creative partnership in an earlier interview with Side-Line.

items.title: Robert Calvert’s ‘Hype’ reissued on vinyl by Cleopatra Records
items.summary: Robert Calvert's 1981 album "Hype" returns on vinyl, CD and digital via Cleopatra Records on 27 November 2026, with new artwork and eight CD bonus tracks.
items.fullText:
Robert Calvert, the South African-born singer, poet and former Hawkwind frontman, sees his 1981 rock album “Hype” reissued by Cleopatra Records on 27 November 2026. The reissue arrives on limited edition colored vinyl, in blue or pink, plus CD and digital, with new cover artwork. Both the vinyl and CD editions also reproduce the original 1981 sleeve inside an accompanying booklet.

“Hype” is subtitled “The Songs of Tom Mahler,” a tie-in to Calvert’s own novel of the same name, published by New English Library in 1981. Both album and book follow Tom Mahler, a fictional rock star, through what Calvert described as “what happens to a young band that is exploited by a record company and internal power struggles between two over-ambitious individuals, who use this band as an elaborate game of spy vs. spy.” He conceived it as a comedy as much as a thriller, citing P.G. Wodehouse as a model for the tone he wanted.

“I wanted to write about the music business in the late seventies the way he wrote about Hollywood in the twenties. Although the plot is very much a sort of fast moving thriller type, it has got elements of black humor and sarcasm.”

Calvert wrote every song on the album himself. He has said the album’s songs grew out of the book as he wrote it, title by title: “I didn’t actually plan to do an album of the book until I was about a quarter of the way into it… I had to keep inventing song titles to make it credible. Every time I thought of a song title, it seemed necessary to quote a line from it, and suddenly it took place as a song.” He also rejected any direct real-world models for the story’s characters, saying the album “isn’t based on my own experiences as such,” though it is “derived obviously from stuff I picked up hanging around record companies.”

The backing musicians on “Hype” included three of Calvert’s former Hawkwind bandmates: saxophonist Nik Turner, Michael Moorcock on 12-string guitar, and Simon House on keyboards and violin, all adding backing vocals as well. High Tide’s Peter Pavli played cello, Inner City Unit’s Trev Thoms played lead guitar, and three members of the new wave band Bethnal, who had supported Hawkwind on its 1977 UK tour, rounded out the sessions alongside keyboardist George Csapo, rhythm guitarist Nick Michaels and drummer Pete Dowling. Among the album’s songs is “We Like to Be Frightened,” written and first recorded, then shelved, by Hawkwind during the sessions for 1979’s “PXR5,” Calvert’s final album with the band.

The reissue’s own publicity describes the November 27 vinyl pressing as “Hype”‘s first since 1981. A UK vinyl and CD edition on See For Miles Records also exists, dated September 1989.

The original ‘Hype’ tracklist, plus eight CD bonus tracks

  1. “Over My Head”
  2. “Ambitious”
  3. “It’s the Same”
  4. “Hanging Out on the Seafront”
  5. “Sensitive”
  6. “Evil Rock”
  7. “We Like to Be Frightened”
  8. “Teen Ballad of Deano”
  9. “Flight 105”
  10. “The Luminous Green Glow of the Dials of the Dashboard (At Night)”
  11. “Greenfly and the Rose”
  12. “Lord of the Hornets”

The CD edition adds eight bonus tracks: the previously unreleased studio out-take “Couldn’t Go On,” a rough demo of “Over My Head,” an alternate version of “Hanging Out on the Seafront,” an instrumental demo of “Flight 105,” a demo of “Lord of the Hornets,” a remix of “Lord of the Hornets” by The Damned’s Rat Scabies, a 28 January 1982 live recording of “Evil Rock” from London’s Acklam Hall, and a 1981 Newsbeat interview segment.

“Hype” was originally released in September 1981 on Calvert’s own A-Side Records label, which folded soon afterward, limiting the album’s circulation at the time. The new edition is available to order through Cleopatra Records and on Bandcamp, where it ships alongside a digital download.

About Robert Calvert

Robert Newton Calvert was born on 9 March 1945 in Pretoria, South Africa, and moved to England with his parents at the age of two. After school in London and Margate, he worked as a poet and street performer, founding the theater group Street Dada Nihilismus in 1967 and later publishing poetry in the science-fiction magazine New Worlds, where he befriended author Michael Moorcock.

Calvert joined Hawkwind in 1971 as lyricist and performance poet, a role he took through his childhood friendship with the band’s co-founder Nik Turner. He left for two years, rejoined as Hawkwind’s principal lead vocalist in 1975, and directed the band’s 1972-73 “Space Ritual” tour. He co-wrote the band’s hit single “Silver Machine,” which reached number three on the UK Singles Chart, and left Hawkwind again in 1979 after the “PXR5” album.

Alongside his work with Hawkwind, Calvert built a solo catalog that mixed concept albums with poetry, prose and stage plays. His debut, “Captain Lockheed and the Starfighters,” came out in 1974, followed by “Lucky Leif and the Longships” in 1975, both featuring contributions from producer Brian Eno. “Hype” followed in 1981, paired with his only published novel, and he closed out his studio discography with “Freq” in 1985 and “Test-Tube Conceived” in 1986. Calvert died of a heart attack on 14 August 1988 in Ramsgate, England, at the age of 43.

Cleopatra Records has worked through Calvert’s catalog in recent reissues, including a first-time vinyl pressing of his 1987 cassette release “The Cellar Tapes,” and has a box set, “The Sonic Space Box,” planned for next year. The “Hype” reissue puts one of his most personal projects, a novel and an album built from the same story, back in print on vinyl for the first time in decades.

items.title: The Ordure release ‘Fisch’ single with a Rogue Unit remix
items.summary: The Ordure release "Fisch" on DressCode Black, paired with a Rogue Unit remix, ahead of the duo's BIMfest 2026 opening set.
items.fullText:
Belgian industrial tribal noise project The Ordure has released “Fisch”, a single on the Antwerp label DressCode Black, paired with a remix from Rogue Unit. DressCode Black’s announcement sets the single for streaming platforms on 4 December 2026; “Fisch” appeared on the label’s Bandcamp page on 22 November, the same pattern the label followed when it put the “Red” EP up on Bandcamp more than a week ahead of that record’s own streaming date.

Frederik Strobbe produced “Fisch”, with lyrics and vocals by Jan De Paepe; Detroit-Berlin handled mixing and mastering. Rogue Unit, Strobbe’s industrial techno project also known for Darkvolt and ATOMS inc., reworks the track into what the label describes as a more club-oriented production built on pounding rhythms and heavy low-end, retaining the original’s repeating rhythmic structure.

The Ordure opens BIMfest 2026 on Saturday 5 December, and the band was recently interviewed by Dark Entries Magazine about its musical approach and influences.

The Ordure’s ‘Fisch’ tracklist

  1. Fisch (Radio Edit)
  2. Fisch (Rogue Unit Remix)

“Fisch” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp.

About The Ordure

The Ordure is a Belgian industrial project formed by Frederik Strobbe and Jan De Paepe, operating under the banner of Industrial Tribal Noise. The duo combines raw, repetitive rhythms, dark electronic textures and German-language vocals, drawing on industrial, electro and tribal influences. Strobbe also records as Rogue Unit and as Darkvolt and ATOMS inc., acts whose own singles and albums have appeared on DressCode Black alongside releases by CauseNation and Deadly Sins.

“Fisch” follows The Ordure’s “Das Dritte Auge” single and “Zeig!” EP on DressCode Black, and arrives as the duo prepares to open BIMfest 2026.

items.title: Deadly Sins release ‘Ghosts’ single with two remixes
items.summary: Deadly Sins release "Ghosts" on DressCode Black, backed by remixes from NER\OGRIS and CauseNation.
items.fullText:
Belgian dark electro project Deadly Sins has released “Ghosts”, a single on the Antwerp label DressCode Black, backed by remixes from NER\OGRIS and CauseNation. DressCode Black’s announcement sets the single for streaming platforms on 24 December 2026; “Ghosts” appeared on the label’s Bandcamp page on 22 November, the same pattern the label followed when it put the “Red” EP up on Bandcamp more than a week ahead of that record’s own streaming date.

C.VII produced “Ghosts” and Arnte handled the mastering, the same production pairing behind Deadly Sins’ “Red” EP and “Mad Mind of This World” album. NER\OGRIS contributes a reworking described by the label as moving between dark atmospheres and dancefloor-oriented electronics; CauseNation, a Belgian EBM and electro-industrial project, built its version on harder rhythms and melodic elements layered over the original’s vocal line.

Deadly Sins’ ‘Ghosts’ tracklist

  1. Ghosts
  2. Ghosts (NER\OGRIS Remix)
  3. Ghosts (CauseNation Remix)

“Ghosts” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp.

About Deadly Sins

Deadly Sins is the solo dark electro project of Cyrb.VII, also known for the Belgian EBM duo WULF7, whose own catalogue includes the album “Dark Hate” (2021) and the “I Don’t Want Anymore” EP (2022). Cyrb.VII set up Deadly Sins afterward, releasing several EPs before the debut album “Mad Mind of This World” in April 2026, a 13-track record built more around atmosphere and string arrangements than the pounding beats typical of EBM. DressCode Black followed that album with the six-track “Red” EP in August 2026, pairing the title track with an alternate version and four remixes, again produced by C.VII with mastering by Arnte.

“Ghosts” extends the same working relationship with DressCode Black, adding NER\OGRIS and CauseNation to the label’s growing list of artists who have remixed Deadly Sins’ material.

items.title: Melting Rust Opera releases ‘Dark Light Damage’ album on Dark Daze Music
items.summary: German industrial act Melting Rust Opera releases its new album "Dark Light Damage" via Dark Daze Music, following collaborations with Carlos Perón.
items.fullText:
German industrial rock act Melting Rust Opera has released its new album, “Dark Light Damage”, via Dark Daze Music on 18 November 2026. The ten-track record is the project’s first solo full-length since its collaborations with Carlos Perón, the Swiss musician and founding member of Yello.

“Dark Light Damage” runs ten tracks in just under 33 minutes, opening with “Interupted Species” and closing with “Queen And King”. Melting Rust Opera is centered around Stefan Bahners, who handles vocals and lyrics for the project.

Melting Rust Opera’s ‘Dark Light Damage’ tracklist

  1. Interupted Species
  2. You Cover Yourself In Machines
  3. I Can’t Say Anything
  4. Between Us
  5. Greytyll
  6. Waiting
  7. Bodyhorror
  8. In The Storm
  9. You Want Me To Fall
  10. Queen And King

“Dark Light Damage” is available to stream on Spotify.

About Melting Rust Opera

Melting Rust Opera is a German industrial project centered around Stefan Bahners, fusing metal and industrial influences. The project has produced remixes for Anne Clark, Burton C Bell of Fear Factory, A Place to Bury Strangers, The Wedding Present, Dagobert and Laibach.

Bahners went on to collaborate with Carlos Perón, who co-founded Yello in Zurich in 1979 alongside Boris Blank and Dieter Meier before leaving the group in 1983 for a solo career. Perón and Melting Rust Opera released the single “Start Again” in May 2025, with Perón producing and Bahners providing vocals and lyrics, followed by the single “I’m a Ghost”. The collaboration grew into the debut album “Ultra Haunted Overdrive”, released on 7 August 2026 through Dark Daze Music, gathering the two singles with eight further tracks the pair produced over roughly a year.

“Dark Light Damage” follows that collaboration as Melting Rust Opera’s own album release on Dark Daze Music.

items.title: OBSEXED preview second album with ‘Night Reverbs’ cassette
items.summary: OBSEXED's "Night Reverbs" cassette, out via Detriti Records, previews the Italian duo's second album with five new tracks.
items.fullText:
Italian post-punk duo OBSEXED has released “Night Reverbs”, a five-track cassette the band describes as a preview of its upcoming second album. Detriti Records, the Berlin label, issued the tape on 1 October 2026.

“Night Reverbs” was written, performed and recorded by OBSEXED between 2025 and 2026, and mixed and mastered by Maurizio Baggio at La Distilleria. Bandcamp credits list the band as Marco Scarabel and Giuseppe Taibi, a change from the Scarabel-Casarrubia line-up credited on the band’s debut album.

OBSEXED’s ‘Night Reverbs’ tracklist

  1. Dry
  2. Sirens
  3. Closer
  4. Insomniac
  5. Safe Haven

“Night Reverbs” is available as a limited-edition cassette via Detriti Records.

About OBSEXED

Marco Scarabel founded OBSEXED in Italy during the isolation of the pandemic lockdowns, recording his first material alone. The project’s earliest work, the single “Five Days” backed with “Too Much Spring Into This Cold Night”, was released digitally in 2022.

Angelo Casarrubia joined as the band’s second member for the debut album “The Wedding”, released on 20 September 2024 in two editions: a full CD version through Industrial Complexx, and a vinyl edition through Oráculo Records carrying a shorter tracklist plus the two 2022 single tracks. Scarabel and Casarrubia had previously played together in Buzz Aldrin and Bromance.

For “Night Reverbs”, OBSEXED’s Bandcamp credits list the duo as Marco Scarabel and Giuseppe Taibi. The five-track cassette marks the band’s first release through Detriti Records and its first new material since “The Wedding”.

items.title: ‘Mythology’ Prague: Žaneta Endlicherová and Richard Schneider on musical curiosity and the freedom to listen
items.summary: Schloss Tegal's Richard Schneider and Mythology founder Žaneta Endlicherová discuss the Prague event ahead of its 28 November 2026 edition.
items.fullText:
Mythology, the Prague event built around experimental electronics, industrial and noise, holds its 2026 edition on 28 November at Subzero in Prague. Ahead of the show, Karo Kratochwil spoke with festival founder Žaneta Endlicherová (DJ Deus Ex Machina) and Richard Schneider, the musician behind Schloss Tegal, about the event’s origins, their different musical backgrounds and why they built a line-up around contrast.

Endlicherová founded Mythology in Prague in 2006 with little knowledge of industrial or noise music and no plan to build a festival around either genre. Her interests at the time lay in electro-dub, emerging dubstep and Oriental music, and the event grew out of curiosity about music that resisted easy recognition.

A turning point came in 2010, when she met Schneider, the American musician behind Schloss Tegal. His collection of experimental, industrial and post-punk recordings introduced her to a different musical history, and their relationship became part of Mythology’s development, continuing after the event’s return in 2025.

The 28 November 2026 edition at Subzero brings together John Duncan, TeZ, Tábor Radosti and Adolphobitch, alongside Endlicherová’s own DJ set as Deus Ex Machina. The festival’s promotional poster lists JTNB Monggo as the fifth act on the bill; Kratochwil’s accompanying introduction names Hecate instead.

Žaneta Endlicherová and Richard Schneider interview

Karo: Žaneta, you founded Mythology in 2006, when experimental electronics, industrial and noise occupied a rather different position in underground culture. What originally attracted you to unconventional music, and what prompted you to establish the event? Was there something you felt was missing from Prague’s musical landscape?

Žaneta: I was 28 when I started Mythology. I had always been part of underground culture and avoided the mainstream, the bands selling out sports stadiums and the music you hear on the radio. I was looking for music that could surprise my ears, something unexpected, strange and different.

But in 2006, I was listening to quite different things. I adored electro-dub, I was discovering dubstep, I loved Oriental music, and I was still very much into dancing, really dancing, all night until the clubs closed. My nights were about being out from dusk till dawn, either DJing or partying.

The first artist I invited was Serhat Köksal, who performs as 2/5 BZ, from Istanbul. His music, videos and messages were so messy, weird and difficult to grasp that they immediately caught my attention. I found that fascinating.

I had no vision or strategy for Mythology back then, and I knew very little about industrial or noise music. I was happy with the musical world I was living in. I didn’t feel anything was missing in Prague. Mythology wasn’t born out of a need to fill a gap; it grew out of curiosity and the excitement of discovering something I couldn’t easily make sense of.

Karo: You come from different musical backgrounds and generations of underground culture. Which artists, recordings or experiences fundamentally changed the way you listen to music? And after so many years together, do your musical interests tend to converge, or do you still challenge each other’s tastes?

Žaneta: Oh yes. We definitely come from very different musical backgrounds and generations. What fundamentally changed the way I listen to music was 2010, when I met Richard (Schloss Tegal), who was a fan of my DJ sets. We were both single, and he asked me for a date. Then an adventure began.

Just after we moved in together, he had to leave Czechia for 90 days because his visa was only valid for that period. During his last stay in the US, he shipped his entire record collection to my studio: approximately 1,000 vinyl records.

The shipment ended up lost in Austria instead of Czechia. Only thanks to my own detective work, and with the help of a Czech friend who speaks fluent German, were we able to track it down and have it redirected to Prague and released from customs. A friend then helped me carry the boxes up to the attic, five floors, via narrow stairs, to my studio, where I was living at the time.

Richard was in the USA, and there I was, sitting in a room full of Whitehouse, Throbbing Gristle, SPK, Maurizio Bianchi, Nurse With Wound, Esplendor Geométrico, Nocturnal Emissions, Pere Ubu, Lustmord, Conrad Schnitzler, Pierre Henry, Klaus Schulze and Iannis Xenakis, among others. An enormous collection of post-punk, noise and industrial music.

My tastes changed. I dropped everything I had been into before, and a new world of ideas opened up for me.

Now, after 16 years together, I think I’m the one challenging him musically. He thinks he’s heard everything there is to hear, but I keep proving him wrong. There’s always something new out there that he’s never heard before, and I love that.

Karo: Richard, you first performed at Mythology alongside Tábor Radosti in 2012. After the event’s long hiatus and its return in 2025, how has your understanding of its purpose changed? What would you like Mythology to become?

Richard: When I was invited to play at Mythology with Tábor Radosti in 2012, it was the first time I had ever experienced Mythology. Back then, I didn’t know much about it except that it was a party in one of Prague’s notorious clubs.

In 2025, it was resurrected as an organised birthday party, a mini music festival celebration. Sutcliffe No More were the headliners, alongside Thorofon, Vilgoc, DJ Martyn Flash and Schloss Tegal.

That was the catalyst that made us want to continue, after seeing the response from our friends, but on a larger scale. Since Prague is in the centre of Europe, we want Mythology to become an international meeting event for people interested in discovering new and innovative acts.

Karo: Mythology’s motto, “Not Everything Is Meant to Be Understood,” raises an interesting question about how we approach experimental music. We often feel compelled to identify influences, analyse structures and assign meanings to what we hear. Do you believe there are experiences that become more valuable when we stop trying to explain them?

Žaneta: Oh yes, of course. I wish you could come to Mythology and simply listen to the sounds of the music you’ll hear there, and somehow just feel them.

I’m not going to tell you how to feel. That’s entirely up to you. It’s one of the small freedoms you have in this world: to listen with your own ears and be free to experience it without thinking about what musical style it belongs to, why it was composed that way, or why you don’t hear drums or a conventional rhythm in certain tracks.

It’s natural for human beings to keep asking why. But what about simply stopping for a moment and listening? Feeling? And even after the music is over, you don’t have to judge it immediately or try to interpret it.

It’s like food. When you’re eating something delicious, just enjoy the experience; you don’t need to think about the recipe or search for the ingredients. Just eat, experience it with all your senses and enjoy it.

Give yourself a break. You don’t have to understand everything and everyone. The need to understand, categorise and analyse everything prevents us from simply experiencing it. And not everything is meant to be understood.

Karo: John Duncan has spent decades exploring the boundaries between sound art, performance, psychological confrontation and subjects that many people would prefer not to examine. What makes his work particularly relevant to Mythology, and do you think genuinely confrontational art can still challenge an audience accustomed to increasingly extreme imagery and information?

Žaneta: First, let us ask ourselves what a myth actually is. Is it necessarily an ancient story, a god or a ritual? Or can we also understand mythology as a system of beliefs, fears, taboos and collective representations through which we attempt to make sense of what it means to be human?

In Duncan’s work, I see an exploration of precisely these territories: the body, sexuality, violence, fear, desire, obsession, death and self-punishment. His subject matter touches upon something deeply rooted in the human experience, something that has always been present in mythology, rituals and the collective unconscious.

Duncan creates a situation in which we are confronted with our own reactions, our own boundaries and our prejudices.

I can relate to this on a personal level. From a young age, people simply would not leave me alone. They attributed all kinds of unfounded accusations to me. They constantly put words into my mouth, associated me with ideas that were completely contrary to my own, and told stories about me that had never happened. There seemed to be an almost relentless need to put me into a category, to define me, without ever bothering to find out who I actually was.

For me, prejudice belongs in the same category as envy, ill will and self-centredness. These are among the worst human qualities.

I am not an expert on John Duncan’s work, but I don’t think he ever set out to shock anyone. Yes, his art is confrontational. If someone finds it shocking, then so be it; that is a matter of individual perception.

Personally, I enjoy confrontation. I enjoy the way it challenges my established assumptions and disrupts the way I have become accustomed to perceiving things. There is very little in art that can genuinely shock me.

What shocks me is the state of the world and the horrors of everyday reality: ongoing genocides, the deaths of innocent victims of wars, the suffering we are exposed to or witness every day. It has become so commonplace, so relentlessly present in our lives, that we seem to have developed an immunity to the sheer magnitude of the evil of our time. Art and music cannot shock me any more. For me, ordinary everyday life is what is truly shocking.

I am drawn to the work of musicians and artists who can take me somewhere I would never have ventured on my own, and John Duncan is one of them. He explored himself, and put himself through suffering and pain primarily upon himself. The fact that we happen to be watching is our own choice. I would say we do not necessarily need to analyse Duncan at all, but we can, if we choose to, and in the process perhaps discover something about ourselves. Perhaps the most provocative thing art can do is not to shock us with something we have never seen before, but to make us recognise something within ourselves that we have never wanted to see.

Karo: TeZ has an extensive history in experimental electronic music and has worked with Clock DVA for many years, yet his independent projects explore a remarkably diverse range of technological and perceptual possibilities. What attracted you to his work, and how did he become part of this year’s programme?

Žaneta: TeZ has been a permanent member of Clock DVA since 2010. Everyone who knows Clock DVA knows Adi Newton, of course, but hardly anyone seems to know the “other” guy.

To me, TeZ is a remarkable musician and a unique artist. When I discovered his latest projects, PRAGMA, SARMUNG, LITEZ and Black BAMBOO, I fell in love with his work, so I invited him to perform. I didn’t approach him primarily from the perspective of whether he fitted the overall philosophy of my event; I was genuinely drawn to his work, and that was reason enough for me.

Karo: The programme also features Tábor Radosti and Adolphobitch, two projects with quite different approaches to industrial expression. How important is it for you to maintain a connection with the Czech underground while bringing together artists from other countries? And what determines which musicians you invite?

Žaneta: I chose Tábor Radosti because I always want to have at least one Czech band in my line-up. I’m Czech, and the festival takes place in Czechia, so this feels important to me. I also like their work and believe they deserve more attention than they currently receive.

Adolphobitch is a project by Matthias Beisl, who also organised his own festival in Linz, Austria. I was there three times, twice as a DJ myself. Through his festival Tormentum, I discovered music and projects I would probably never have come across on my own. I encountered Sutcliffe No More live for the first time there, and they later played at my last Mythology.

All the music we are describing here belongs to a specific niche scene, so it’s natural that we should stick together and support each other. It’s good to stay within familiar circles and keep returning to the musical territories you already know, but it’s equally important to remain curious, explore unfamiliar waters and create opportunities to discover things beyond your usual horizon.

Karo: This year’s programme moves between experimental sound art, ritual industrial, noise and breakcore, styles that demand quite different forms of attention and listening. Do you deliberately seek such contrasts, or do you hear a deeper connection between musical approaches that might initially seem incompatible?

Žaneta: Yes, exactly. I deliberately seek that kind of contrast. I think the approaches are incompatible, but I like challenging the listeners. I want to wake up their attention.

I want people who would never go to see one of the artists on the line-up if they were performing separately to see and hear them anyway, and to be challenged by it. I want them to hear something different from what they are used to, something outside their comfort zone. I don’t like it when people simply don’t go to see anything except the things they already know.

Karo: Richard, your work with Schloss Tegal has long explored recorded environments, psychological states and the relationship between sound and perception. Žaneta, you also approach music through your work as a DJ, but your listening experiences are clearly very personal. When encountering unfamiliar music, what attracts each of you most: composition, texture, physical impact, atmosphere or the possibility of hearing something genuinely original?

Žaneta: It’s important to distinguish between listening to music and presenting it as a DJ to an audience; they are two different things.

Listening, for me, means being aware of composition, thinking about it deeply and feeling the texture. It is a physical experience, because music has the power to make me cry. When I’m listening to music at home or through my headphones, I breathe faster, I smile, I think, I rethink, I wonder, I cry too.

Playing music as a DJ for others is different. I try to create a certain atmosphere for the audience, but it’s more on the surface, interesting tracks and mixes. I want the audience to feel positive and good; I don’t want to make them feel uncomfortable or cry.

Richard: Originality is what I look for in art and music. I am an artist myself, so I’m looking for something that will take me somewhere, someplace shocking, and communicate a message to me. Some musical genres these days are beginning to feel overdone. I’m looking for fresh identities and new genres.

Karo: Twenty years after Mythology began, experimental music is considerably easier to find online, but that doesn’t necessarily mean listeners have become more adventurous. Do you think the increased availability of music has changed the way people approach challenging work? And what would you like someone encountering Mythology for the first time to experience?

Žaneta: I think experimental music is easier to discover in the sense that some of it is now available online, but that doesn’t necessarily make it accessible to a wider audience. It is still mostly discovered by people who already have some knowledge of or interest in it. For someone who has never encountered, say, musique concrète, discovering it in the first place isn’t necessarily easy. I, for example, didn’t fully discover it until 2023.

I wouldn’t say it’s easier to consume without much attention. However elitist that might sound, I feel this music was never really intended to be understood by everyone, but rather to be explored and appreciated by a relatively small audience. And again, not everything is meant to be understood.

About Schloss Tegal and Mythology

Mythology was founded in Prague in 2006 by Žaneta Endlicherová, known as DJ Deus Ex Machina, as an independent event dedicated to experimental electronics, industrial, noise, breakcore and unconventional musical expression. Endlicherová had no fixed genre plan for the event at its outset; its direction grew from her own listening habits at the time, including electro-dub, dubstep and Oriental music, and from the first act she booked, Istanbul’s Serhat Köksal (2/5 BZ).

Richard Schneider, the American musician behind Schloss Tegal, first performed at Mythology alongside Tábor Radosti in 2012. He and Endlicherová met in 2010, and his collection of industrial, post-punk and noise recordings, including works by Whitehouse, Throbbing Gristle, SPK, Nurse With Wound and Lustmord among others, changed her own listening. Mythology went on hiatus before returning in 2025 as a one-off celebration headlined by Sutcliffe No More, alongside Thorofon, Vilgoc, DJ Martyn Flash and Schloss Tegal; the response from that show led Endlicherová and Schneider to continue the event on a larger scale.

The 28 November 2026 edition takes place at Subzero, Nádražní 3, Prague, with John Duncan, TeZ, Tábor Radosti and Adolphobitch on the bill alongside Endlicherová’s own DJ set as Deus Ex Machina, doors at 19:00. TeZ has been a member of Clock DVA since 2010 alongside Adi Newton, and also records as PRAGMA, SARMUNG, LITEZ and Black BAMBOO. Adolphobitch is the project of Matthias Beisl, who also runs the Tormentum festival in Linz, Austria. Tickets and line-up information are available through the event’s ticket page.

items.title: KIFOTH interview: ‘Without hope, I would not have the strength to uphold the conviction that there is a way forward’
items.summary: Since their formation in 1993, the Slovakian act KIFOTH (Kneel In Front Of The Hangman)...
items.fullText:
Since their formation in 1993, the Slovakian act KIFOTH (Kneel In Front Of The Hangman) has carved out a distinct niche within the European EBM and Industrial scene. What began as a project founded by K-Head and Mir Colon has evolved over the years from raw, uncompromising EBM into a multifaceted Electronic sound, increasingly embracing Industrial textures, Experimental elements, and dark atmospheric layers. With albums released on labels such as Out Of Line, Vendetta Music, EK Product and now Aliens Production, the band has established a distinctive identity without ever confining itself to a single style. Following a period of relative silence, KIFOTH returned with “Lost Territory”, followed by “Artificial Territory” – an album in which existing compositions were reworked through Experimental production techniques, including AI-driven processes. Today, KIFOTH continues to push its musical boundaries, with a renewed live lineup and a sound that combines its original EBM roots with fresh Electronic influences. I sat down with the band to discuss their musical evolution, creative collaborations, and what the future holds for KIFOTH. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries)

KIFOTH interview

SL: You have been active as KIFOTH for over 30 years, and a great deal has happened during that time—from personal developments and musical evolution to collaborations with various labels, the addition of a new member, and major changes in the world around you. How do you look back on this journey, and how do you see your lives and roles as artists today compared to when you first started making music?

mir Colon: mir Colon does exist thanks to KIFOTH. I love the unique dimension in which mir Colon operates, whilst at the same time having a positive influence on my everyday life. The contemporary art scene has many more dimensions than it did in the nineties. Ultimately, this has led to the brutal relentlessness of the song’s life cycle and the principle of consumerism.

SL: Last year saw the release of “Lost Territory”, which, after years of silence, featured four new tracks, followed by a series of remixes of older material. Let’s start by discussing those new tracks. What prompted you to start creating new music after such a long period of inactivity? What were your main sources of inspiration, and how did the tracks take shape?

Keyhead: Yes, it has been quite a long time since the previous KIFOTH release, but not for me personally. I’ve been active in several bands and involved in production and remix work. During what could be called the long break following the “Extensive Report” album, I actually wrote a lot of material. With the project Eclipsed, we released two albums on the Aliens Production and Electrofrequent labels.

Eclipsed is a collaborative project with members of Samhain and a few special guests, including Don Gordon from Numb and James Mendez from Jihad. It’s quite experimental and focused on pure electronics.

I also wrote and co-produced the two most recent albums by the Czech EBM band Vanessa, where I eventually became a full member. I also joined them on two years of touring, which took up a lot of my time.

There was actually a lot of material ready, but it was important to find the right mood and sound that would work with Mir Colon’s lyrics and feel right for a release under the KIFOTH name. I think everything finally came together, and the songs now fit perfectly, both musically and lyrically, to deliver the message we wanted to convey.

SL: This year, you followed up with “Artificial Territory”, featuring your own remixes of the four new tracks. How did this idea come about, and what did the remixing process involve? Where did you draw your inspiration from, and how did your ideas evolve during the process? What are the main differences in terms of approach, sound design, and production between the original versions and these new interpretations?

Keyhead: Yeah, that idea came to me immediately after hearing the remixes by my friends who contributed to the “Lost Territory” album. I was really excited to hear how they had transformed the sound and arrangements of the KIFOTH tracks. It made me wonder how differently they could reinterpret the music we had created.

At the same time, I had started experimenting with AI tools the previous year. I realized that AI isn’t really the right tool for generating completely new songs, ideas, or riffs, but it can be very useful for inspiration and certain aspects of the production process.

I have to say that, in real life, AI is a great tool for making perfect whisky, but it will never create the grain. As our original idea was to create a remix album rather than write new songs, I was convinced that this release would sound completely different from the original.

I reopened the original recording session projects and started experimenting with AI tools on some of the individual instrument stems, using them to regenerate and reinterpret certain elements. The idea was to recreate some of the original riffs in a different way, using the actual music as a starting point. That’s also what explains the album title, “Artificial Territory”.

Most of the stems and sound design elements come from the original album tracks, but some portions of every track have been replaced or transformed. The main melodies and lyrics remain the same, and even the vocal articulation is largely preserved, although the interpretation has changed.

Initially, we still used Mir Colon’s original vocals, but eventually, to make the album more experimental and colourful, we decided to regenerate the vocals on some tracks as well, replacing them with female voices. And I like the result a lot!

Of course, once you start changing the production and introducing new stems, you inevitably need to rewrite certain passages, completely rethink fills and bass lines, and make other adjustments to preserve the originality of each track rather than simply relying on repetitive, AI-generated loops.

It was a really fun workflow, and I think it’s quite useful as a source of inspiration, although I wouldn’t recommend using it as the foundation for creating music. Turning the results into something that follows the author’s concept and the desired structure requires almost as much work as composing a track from scratch. Sometimes it’s even more complicated!

SL: Throughout your career, KIFOTH has consistently maintained a critical perspective on society and the world we live in. With “Lost Territory”, however, there seems to be a growing sense of concern, perhaps even fear, about where things are heading and what we will leave behind for future generations. Could you elaborate on the ideas behind these lyrics? Do you still see any grounds for optimism, or do you believe we are approaching a point of no return?

mir Colon: The “Lost Territory” concept focuses primarily on the crises facing the modern world and the depletion of resources. The lyrics are not in the style of conventional song lyrics. I deliberately aimed to create journalistic columns. A straightforward presentation of facts, a call for participants to take an interest in issues such as the impending scarcity of natural resources, the climate crisis and the energy crisis. Demographics, health and ageing, geopolitics and the future of the world. Technological progress and its risks: artificial intelligence, biotechnology, genetic modification, and the question of whether society can ethically and safely manage their rapid development.

Without hope, I would not have the strength to uphold the conviction that there is a way forward. I portray the present as a chain of interconnected crises — environmental, energy, demographic, technological and political. At the same time, I support well-known theories, such as the circular economy, clean technologies, international cooperation and, above all, the individual responsibility of every person.

SL: I have always found it fascinating when artists—musicians and other creative minds alike—work around a particular theme or concept. How does this process unfold for you? Does a theme emerge naturally as the music takes shape, or does the initial concept determine the composition, atmosphere, sound design, and overall direction of a track?

mir Colon: In most cases, the concept and the sound composition emerge independently in the early stages. Our work is inspired by present-day stimuli and themes. We’ve been friends since our school days. By this I mean to say that there is an exceptional connection between us – something like a special data channel. Through this channel, we share the initial ideas with one another, and the journey towards creating the final composition is a process of interweaving, complementing, reshaping… but above all, of fascinating emotional and energetic waves. Once again, and as always, I am fascinated by just how much energy and emotion we manage to capture in the final recording.

SL: You have been involved with KIFOTH for many years, while also pursuing various side projects. How do you distinguish between these different musical outlets, and do you consider any of them your main project? Are you currently working on new material or exploring other creative directions? What are your plans and ambitions for the future, both individually and as KIFOTH?

Keyhead: I enjoy many different kinds and subgenres of Electronic music, and each has its own characteristic structures and elements. Since I collaborate with musicians and singers who have their own specific tastes and styles, I always try to adapt my approach and production accordingly.

You can hear examples of my production work on Vanessa albums such as “Ghost Army” and “Škleb”, as well as on various remixes and cover versions. Eclipsed, for example, is a project where my main contribution is in creating melodies, samples, loops, and drum patterns.

In parallel, I started performing live with my own ambient solo project, Keyhead, and I’m planning to release an album soon, hopefully around New Year. It consists of material reflecting different personal moods and experiences collected over the past seven years. The project is more focused on Ambient music and a kind of film scoring.

KIFOTH will definitely remain my main project for the future. However, things tend to move a little more slowly than with my other projects because there are clearer structural requirements and compromises regarding how the songs and albums should sound and develop, as well as more people involved in the creative process.

We already have some new material in place, but following the release of “Lost Territory”, we’ve mainly been focusing on live shows, with more dates planned. And I’m really enjoying that!

With our new member Blažena from Samhain, who plays live drums during our shows, we’ve basically been rearranging our older tracks for every tour. We want to make room for the drums while also ensuring that the overall sound fits in with our newer material. We already have several shows confirmed through next June, and I think that after that we’ll be able to dedicate all our time to working on new material, which we hopefully plan to release in the second half of 2028.

Until then, I wish all the best to Side-Line and all our fans. I’m sure we’ll meet again at some live shows in the meantime!

About KIFOTH

KIFOTH formed in Slovakia in 1993 as Kneel In Front Of The Hangman, a project built around K-Head (now performing as Keyhead) on music and Mir Colon on vocals. The duo’s first live show took place in 1994 at the “Young Apollo” festival, as recounted in a 2017 Side-Line interview. After a run of self-released albums, two albums followed on Out Of Line and two more on Vendetta Music; Side-Line’s own archive from that period refers to the project as Kneel In Front Of The Executioner, before the band settled on the KIFOTH name. The debut album, “Spectaclebreakers,” was released in 1999, and “Extensive Report” followed on EK Product.

The live album “Alive:d,” recorded during the 2017 “Extinction Of Mankind” tour, was released in January 2020 on the band’s own label. After six years without new studio material, KIFOTH returned in November 2025 with “Lost Territory,” its first release for the Bratislava-based label Aliens Production: four new tracks plus nine remixes contributed by Samhain, Last Influence Of Brain, Sleepwalk, Disharmony, The Opposer Divine, Terminal State, Brain Leisure, Deflect and The Witch Said No.

The follow-up, “Artificial Territory,” followed on CD and digital on June 11, 2026. It revisited the four “Lost Territory” tracks plus an older song from “Spectaclebreakers” in ten new mixes produced by the band itself, mastered by Anatoly “Tokee” Grinberg with design by Housecore, and was reviewed by Side-Line in October 2026. The band’s current studio and live lineup lists Keyhead, Mir Colon and drummer Blažena, formerly of Samhain, who joined for the act’s recent touring. This interview follows that lineup and release history, with KIFOTH discussing its musical evolution and plans for new material.

items.title: Maciek Szymczuk – Gandobendy (Digital/CD Album – Zoharum)
items.summary: Maciek Szymczuk has been active under his own name for over 20 years, yet it...
items.fullText:
Maciek Szymczuk has been active under his own name for over 20 years, yet it has taken nearly 9 years for this new album to arrive. The work feels as though it were inspired by an imaginary dreamscape—a state of mind that traverses various worlds.

Musically, this has been translated into 7 tracks that, from the very first moment, serve as an invitation to explore a diverse sonic landscape. Ranging from Minimal-Electro loops to pieces defined by deep, vibrating bass tones—and venturing into pure Cinematic music before embracing more uninhibited experimentation toward the end—the album has a great deal to offer. While the addition of a vocal element here and there might have provided an extra dimension, the album stands strong just as it is. Personally, I have a soft spot for the tracks that lean more toward Minimal-Electro.

All in all, this is a powerful album that is sure to put Maciek Szymczuk back on the map. (Rating:8).

Listen to “Elektronytek”:

About Maciek Szymczuk

Maciek Szymczuk is a Polish musician whose solo catalog began in 2002 with the album “Dilmun”. He has since released “Clouds” (2013), “Music For Cassandra” (2015), “The Seer” (2015) and “Light Of The Dreams” (2017) on Zoharum, the album that preceded “Gandobendy” by close to nine years. Szymczuk also records as Aabzu, a project with Łukasz Szałankiewicz (Zenial), and under the names Terminus and Another One, the latter with Kuba Łuka. He has contributed remixes to other Zoharum artists, including two tracks on Moan’s “Isolate / Desolate / Mutate” remix album. “Gandobendy” is a seven-track digital and CD album released on 30 June 2026 through Zoharum, with the CD edition issued as a six-panel ekopack limited to 300 copies.

items.title: ‘Eastside Festival’ 2027 lineup brings Mesh, Kite and Heppner’s TanzZwang to Halle
items.summary: Eastside Festival returns to Karlsbad, Halle (Saale) on 2-3 July 2027 with Mesh, Kite, Heppner's TanzZwang, TRAITRS, Ductape and Then Comes Silence.
items.fullText:
Eastside Festival returns to Halle (Saale), Germany, on 2-3 July 2027, bringing two days of synthpop, EBM, darkwave, post-punk and alternative electronic music to the lakeside setting of Karlsbad at Angersdorfer Teiche. Now entering its fifth year, the festival has announced a lineup combining established names with newer projects, including Mesh, Kite, Heppner’s TanzZwang, TRAITRS, Ductape, Then Comes Silence, T.O.Y., DSTR, The Sound Veil Society and Unify Separate.

Organised by Hamburg-based PLUSWELT PROMOTION in cooperation with Karlsbad and Freizeit und Event GmbH, and presented alongside Sonic Seducer, Eastside Festival originated as an idea during the pandemic. Since then, it has developed into a regular meeting point for audiences interested in alternative electronic music, favouring a relatively intimate atmosphere over the scale of larger European festivals. Its unusual location, with a sandy beach, lakeside views and camping facilities, provides a rather different environment for a programme devoted to darker sounds.

Eastside Festival 2027 headliners: Mesh and Kite

Among the leading names for 2027 are Mesh, the British electronic duo whose combination of melodic synthpop, sophisticated production and emotionally direct songwriting has earned them a longstanding international following. Their appearance follows the release of “The Truth Doesn’t Matter” in March 2026, their first studio album in nearly a decade. The record addresses contemporary uncertainty, fractured relationships and the uneasy relationship between truth and perception, extending the band’s familiar musical vocabulary into a new period of creative activity.

Swedish duo Kite, consisting of Nicklas Stenemo and Christian Berg, will also headline the festival. Their music combines dramatic synthesizer arrangements, expansive melodies and an often theatrical approach to live presentation. Their 2024 release “VII,” gathering material from the duo’s series of singles, demonstrated the breadth of their electronic songwriting, including collaborations with Blanck Mass, Anna von Hausswolff and Henric de la Cour. Kite’s concerts have become known for their elaborate visual production, making their appearance an interesting addition to Eastside’s outdoor setting.

Heppner’s TanzZwang, TRAITRS and more join the bill

Another notable booking is Heppner’s TanzZwang, the electronic live project associated with Peter Heppner, whose unmistakable voice has played an important role in German synthpop since his years with Wolfsheim. TanzZwang places greater emphasis on dance-oriented electronic arrangements, moving Heppner’s distinctive vocal style into a more direct club environment.

The darker, guitar-driven side of the programme is represented by TRAITRS, the Canadian post-punk duo whose austere arrangements, insistent rhythms and emotionally charged vocals draw upon the traditions of gothic rock and darkwave. Their music combines an unmistakable connection to earlier post-punk with contemporary production, making them a natural fit for the festival’s broader aesthetic.

Ductape, the Turkish duo formed by Çağla and Furkan Güleray, bring another perspective on contemporary darkwave. Having developed their sound through extensive international touring, they released their fourth album, “Faded Flowers,” in September 2026. Their combination of driving basslines, guitar, synthesizers and expressive vocals has become increasingly distinctive, with the new material exploring alienation, emotional distance and the contradictions of contemporary life.

Sweden’s Then Comes Silence are another important name for post-punk and gothic rock audiences. Led by Alex Svenson, the group have developed a recognisable sound built around bass-driven arrangements, sharp guitar lines and a strong melodic sensibility. Their eighth studio album, “Requiem Ballroom,” released in November 2026 through Metropolis Records, provides fresh material for a band whose live performances retain a direct connection to gothic rock’s darker, more physical traditions.

The electronic selection extends further with DSTR, the project of Daniel Myer, whose extensive work with Haujobb, Architect and numerous other collaborations has made him one of the most active figures in contemporary electro-industrial music. DSTR offers a more melodic and dance-oriented outlet for his production interests, retaining the detailed electronic construction associated with his other projects while approaching songwriting from a different perspective.

T.O.Y. add another established name from the German electronic scene, while Unify Separate bring their combination of synthesizer-driven songwriting and expansive alternative influences to the programme. Their third album, “The God Particle,” released in November 2026, further develops the partnership between Andrew Montgomery and Leo Josefsson, balancing melodic accessibility with a more substantial electronic sound.

Another act worth noting is The Sound Veil Society, the Swedish-Norwegian duo of Erlend Eilertsen and Hans-Olof Mattsson. Their debut album, “Things We Kept,” released through Progress Productions in September 2026, introduced a project concerned with detailed electronic arrangements and atmospheric songwriting. Their inclusion reflects Eastside’s interest in presenting newer artists alongside musicians with considerably longer histories.

The lineup also features KY and M/A/T, the latter founded by Matthias Bischoff, formerly of the synthpop and EBM project Cyber. M/A/T’s music draws upon the rhythmic traditions of classic electronic body music, synthpop and dark disco, bringing another dancefloor-oriented element to the festival.

Special performances at Eastside Festival 2027

Beyond the main concerts, Eastside will offer several additional performances designed for the more informal lakeside environment. Elektro All-Stars will present their EBM karaoke concept, already familiar to visitors of the Wave-Gotik-Treffen warm-up events. Vaughn George will perform his interpretations of Depeche Mode songs by the lake, while Kyle Blaqk of Auger is scheduled for a special acoustic set in the same setting.

These smaller performances are an important part of the festival’s character. Instead of concentrating exclusively on the main stage, Eastside makes use of its location to provide opportunities for audiences to experience music in a more relaxed atmosphere, away from the intensity of conventional concert venues.

The Karlsbad site at Angersdorfer Teiche offers a spacious sandy beach, camping facilities and the opportunity to spend the weekend beside the water. For visitors accustomed to experiencing dark electronic music in crowded clubs, former industrial buildings and enclosed festival halls, the combination of open-air concerts, summer evenings and lakeside surroundings provides an appealing change of scenery.

The organisers emphasise that Eastside was conceived primarily as a gathering for audiences interested in alternative music, not as a commercially driven mainstream event. Its programming reflects that approach, bringing together international artists, established scene favourites and newer names whose work spans different branches of electronic and guitar-based alternative music.

With Mesh and Kite leading the bill, Heppner’s TanzZwang adding a club-oriented dimension, and artists such as TRAITRS, Ductape, Then Comes Silence and DSTR broadening the musical selection, Eastside 2027 offers a well-balanced programme for followers of synthpop, EBM, darkwave and post-punk. Its lakeside setting remains one of its most distinctive features, offering a weekend where the music may be dark, but the surroundings are decidedly summery. This is the fifth edition of the festival, following Eastside Festival 2026, which brought Nitzer Ebb, Covenant and Devision Redux to the same site.

Eastside Festival 2027: dates, lineup and tickets

  • Dates: Friday 2 July – Saturday 3 July 2027
  • Venue: Karlsbad, Angersdorfer Teiche 9, 06126 Halle (Saale), Germany
  • Confirmed lineup: Mesh, Kite, Heppner’s TanzZwang, TRAITRS, Ductape, Then Comes Silence, T.O.Y., DSTR, The Sound Veil Society, Unify Separate, KY and M/A/T
  • Special performances: Elektro All-Stars (EBM karaoke), Vaughn George (Depeche Mode interpretations by the lake), Kyle Blaqk of Auger (lakeside acoustic set)
  • Organisers: PLUSWELT PROMOTION, Karlsbad and Freizeit und Event GmbH, with Sonic Seducer as presenting partner

Weekend tickets are available as original printed tickets or print-at-home tickets through the official ticket shop. Separate camping options are also available, subject to availability. More information is on the festival website and the venue’s own site.

items.title: Xotox – ‘Wir hatten doch Träume’ (Digital Single – Infacted Recordings)
items.summary: Xotox releases 'Wir hatten doch Träume', a three-track digital single via Infacted Recordings, out 2 October 2026.
items.fullText:
German industrial electronic project Xotox, led by Andreas Davids, released “Wir hatten doch Träume” (“We Used to Have Dreams”) on 2 October 2026 through Infacted Recordings. The three-track digital single explores the uncertain afterlife of shared dreams, the gradual erosion of emotional intimacy and the troubling realisation that moments once associated with happiness may now exist only in memory.

The title suggests an unfinished conversation, recalling promises and aspirations whose meaning has changed with time. The accompanying release notes describe dreams and longings overwhelmed by “emotional noise,” fading into a pale grey. For an artist whose musical identity has long been associated with rhythmic noise, the expression carries an additional resonance. Here, mechanical repetition and electronic force provide the setting for something more vulnerable: the persistence of memories that refuse to disappear entirely, even as their emotional significance becomes increasingly difficult to grasp.

The title composition draws upon the experience of a particular night that unexpectedly brings forgotten dreams and emotions back to the surface, only for them to slip away once again. Rather than presenting nostalgia as a comforting return to the past, Xotox approaches it as something less reassuring, confronting the distance between what people once imagined their lives might become and what remains of those expectations.

Musically, the release brings Davids’ established interest in forceful electronic rhythms into contact with a more pronounced melodic sensibility. The contrast between the precision of programmed structures and the uncertainty of the subject matter gives the title track an expressive character that extends beyond the physical intensity usually associated with rhythmic noise. The electronics retain their mechanical discipline, while the melodic elements introduce a quieter sense of longing.

The single also includes “Cherophobia” and “Hypnose,” the latter extending beyond seven minutes and accounting for more than half of the release’s total running time. Together, the three compositions form a compact addition to the Xotox catalogue, continuing Davids’ exploration of the relationship between electronic rhythm, atmosphere and emotional expression.

“Wir hatten doch Träume” was created by Xotox at Separate Room, MTH, in 2026, with mastering by Anatoly Grinberg.

Tracklist: 1. Wir hatten doch Träume – 3:30 2. Cherophobia – 3:19 3. Hypnose – 7:17

“Wir hatten doch Träume” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp.

About Xotox

Founded in Germany in 1998 by Andreas Davids, Xotox released several self-published albums between 1998 and 2002 before signing to Pronoize. Its 2003 album “Lichtlos” became the first album by an industrial act to reach number one on the Deutsche Alternative Charts. The track “[PSI]” reached number two on the same chart in 2005, and 2008’s “In den zehn Morgen” spent six weeks at number one. The project built its catalogue around distorted electronic rhythms, aggressive percussion and atmospheric synthesizers, including the compilation “Essentials (Best Of)” in 2016.

Since joining Infacted Recordings in 2019, Xotox has continued to develop its sound through releases including the 2023 album “Ich bin da / Ich funtioniere”, the 2025 album “Particles” and the remix collection “Dokumentation II: Remix” in 2026. Davids discussed the project’s fusion of techno and industrial elements in a 2020 “Click Interview” with Side-Line. “Wir hatten doch Träume” extends that catalogue with a more melodic turn across its three new tracks.

items.title: Robert J Revell interview: ‘Creation is the point’
items.summary: Robert J Revell talks to Side-Line about The SPKtR's European tour, his solo album "Torn Remnants of Nobility" and working with father Graeme Revell.
items.fullText:
There is something almost paradoxical about Robert J Revell. Onstage, he is an extraordinary physical presence, throwing himself into performances with an intensity that can be exhilarating, unsettling and occasionally difficult to watch. Away from the stage, however, he speaks with remarkable openness about humility, family, artistic responsibility and the complicated relationship between creativity and self-worth.

At the 25th anniversary edition of Wrocław Industrial Festival, Karo Kratochwil experienced both sides of his musical work. His solo performance, drawing upon the visceral, psychologically charged material of “Torn Remnants of Nobility”, revealed an artist whose relationship with sound is intensely physical and deeply personal. The following evening, performing alongside his father, industrial music pioneer Graeme Revell, in The SPKtR, he brought that same instinctive energy into a very different creative environment.

The contrast was revealing. Where Graeme approaches composition through carefully developed structures and technological experimentation, Robert introduces an element of unpredictability, allowing the performance to develop through spontaneous physical responses to sound. Their collaboration is built around those differences, bringing two generations and contrasting artistic philosophies into direct contact.

Yet Robert’s interests extend far beyond industrial music. A multi-instrumentalist with a background spanning death metal, thrash, noise, experimental electronics and numerous other genres, he has created an extensive catalogue of largely unreleased recordings. He also builds and dismantles theatre sets, using the same processes of welding, machinery and manual labour that seem strangely appropriate to his musical world.

During the conversation, Robert reflects on the realities of touring, the unexpected responses to his performances, his relationship with Graeme, the emotional foundations of his solo work and the importance of creating without becoming attached to the result.

Robert J Revell interview

Karo: Robert, I had the pleasure of seeing both your solo performance and The SPKtR at Wrocław Industrial Festival. Two very different experiences, both extraordinarily intense. Looking back, what surprised you most about those two nights?

Robert: For a genre where audiences are accustomed to watching a person stand over a table, tweaking a laptop or a mixer, I was surprised to get the feedback “more vocals, less computer”. It’s interesting to me in that I thought “singing” to the audience might come across as rockstar shit. Not very “industrial”. But it makes sense that we all want connection regardless of the context. I’ve been welcomed into this community and I’m very grateful for it, so I try to approach situations with humility. In most areas of my life, but especially here. I’m glad for the feedback because it aligns with my interests for live performance.

Karo: Wrocław also marked the beginning of your European tour with The SPKtR. How has the journey been unfolding so far? Has anything happened onstage that neither you nor Graeme expected?

Robert: When I first heard the tracks live through a PA, it was at WIF. Previously I’d listened to them on my home stereo, which is pretty powerful but nothing by comparison. So when the show started I immediately became energized and viscerally inspired. And that keeps happening every night. That’s how I end up bashing my hands on the cage, or hanging from the lighting rig, or beating the floor with the metal rods. Every night is a surprise for me. I don’t know what I’ll end up doing.

Karo: Touring takes you through so many cities, people and fleeting encounters. When the venues and setlists begin to blur together, what actually stays with you?

Robert: The way the peaks of the waves light up while I look out the porthole of the night ferry. The way the sun plays hide and seek behind the clouds but you don’t know if it’ll come back at all that day. The excited and hopefully inspired faces of the people I’ve gotten to meet. The way it’s only been a couple weeks but my kids look more grown up already.

Karo: Your biography mentions nearly twenty unreleased albums spanning different genres. What made “Torn Remnants of Nobility” the first one you wanted the world to hear? And is there something liberating about creating music without knowing whether anyone will ever listen to it?

Robert: Art should be made with no consideration of its reception. Then it’s pure. One can choose to edit later if deemed necessary. It’s paramount to be genuine and sincere. People can tell right away if you’re not.

The reason I released Torn Remnants was because I was asked. After the 2025 shows in Pordenone and the VOD Fest I was contacted by a few people about a possible release. So I made an album and sent it off. Walter from Klanggalerie was the most excited about it so I went with him. He’s such a genuine music lover and truly kind person, it’s infectious.

I tend to be quite nihilistic about almost everything in life except the people I love and who love me. So “releasing” music never really occurred to me. Who am I to believe “the world needs to hear this”? I make music for myself and that’s enough.

Karo: The album explores violence, shame, regret and some profoundly uncomfortable aspects of human experience. Does transforming these emotions into music change your relationship with them, or is the act of expression itself what matters?

Robert: The act of releasing these emotions in a live setting is what’s important. It’s catharsis. To be honest in front of people where there’s nowhere to hide is irreplaceable. And if it speaks to someone who might feel the same way but may not be able to put it into words then that’s great. I’ve been on the other side of that so many times in my life as an audience member that it’s only fair to attempt to return the favor.

I’ve also released a “game” called Transient Rumination Original Nascence. It’s an answer to the negative vomit of Torn Remnants. So the themes of Torn Remnants have an answer in Transient Rumination. Things that have helped me to deal with those “negative” emotions. It also has a process to write a poem in a few minutes.

I find that when I’ve completed a task, or especially a piece of art, then I can sort of justify breathing the air, and taking up some precious resources as a guest on this planet Earth.

Karo: “Forgiveness in the Face of Regret” closes the album. Forgiveness isn’t necessarily the end of an emotional struggle. What does it mean to you in the context of this record?

Robert: Forgiveness is a battle. In this case it’s forgiveness of self. No one hates like the self. We are the pigs in the slaughterhouse covered in shit, consuming and consuming. The shame and guilt of that begs forgiveness.

Karo: You’ve played everything from death metal and thrash to experimental electronics and noise. Have you ever encountered an emotion or an idea that one musical language simply couldn’t express, forcing you to find another?

Robert: Not yet. But I do tend to keep the musical languages separate. I try to express the emotions at one time, working on one project with one language. Torn Remnants is the most eclectic thing I’ve done. But the genre allows for that in my opinion.

Karo: You also work in theatre construction, building sets from metal and wood, welding and working with heavy machinery. Has that experience changed the way you understand sound?

Robert: I’ve always loved machines and processes. I started with stereo equipment, moved to rebuilding old cars and motorcycles. That’s where the welding came in.

Everything I enjoy is bad for my ears. Building loud engines with no mufflers, fixing and riding motorcycles, playing in bands, going to concerts, building structures and roofing using nail guns and saws.

I attempt to protect my hearing when I can but I enjoy the feeling. So the sounds of machines satisfy a part of me that “music” does. They are one and the same.

Karo: Theatre sets can require enormous amounts of work, only to be dismantled when a production ends. Does knowing that something you’ve created is temporary affect your attachment to it?

Robert: When the show is over, some parts of the set are salvaged and the rest is destroyed and disposed of. That’s my favorite part. To destroy something you’ve created like the Tibetan Buddhist monks and the Dissolution Ceremony is a display of intense appreciation for beauty while almost simultaneously recognizing its temporary nature.

Except rather than brushing away sand I use a sledgehammer.

It’s reflected in how I sign my CD or book. The painting I created for Torn Remnants or the photo I took for Blurred Recollections and Suspended Moments gets covered in Sharpie in a haphazard way to remind myself not to be precious or egotistical about my work.

Karo: When we spoke at Wrocław Industrial Festival, you mentioned that both your parents had always supported your artistic endeavours. Was there a particular moment when their encouragement gave you the confidence to pursue something unconventional?

Robert: I think it’s been constant. My Mum would constantly prepare art projects for us. And I see it with her and my kids. She always has a fun engaging way to teach people that they can do anything. Anything in the world. The confidence she inspires is staggering.

Karo: You were only ten when you discovered “Information Overload Unit” and realised that your father had created music that seemed to reflect what was happening inside your own mind. Did that discovery change your understanding of what music could actually do?

Robert: When I first heard it I just got really excited. Yes yes yes!!! This is it!! I love this!!!! Then weeks later I found out it was him. So when people tell me they’ve been a fan of SPK for decades, I say me too! What an honor it is to be a part of The SPKtR and to play some of the old songs.

Karo: You’ve known Graeme your entire life, but working with someone creatively can reveal unexpected sides of their personality. What’s something you’ve discovered about your father through making music together that you might never have learned otherwise?

Robert: We are extremely similar in so many ways. Mostly in personality. Our approach musically is very different.

He’s always been excited about new possibilities that emerging technology allows. Looking back over his career it’s incredibly obvious to anyone that the sounds he envisioned were right on the cusp of availability. His voice speaks for the future of humanity. A future that hasn’t happened yet but is definitely coming.

On the other hand, my work is deeply personal and in the moment. My performances are the same way. For me the future does not exist and the past is just a memory skewed by my own recollection. Now is all we have.

Karo: Graeme has described you as The SPKtR’s improvisational wildcard. When you’re onstage together, how do you recognise the moment when a composition needs to be challenged rather than followed?

Robert: He has a specific vision for everything. He’s extremely calculated and focused on the details. This is perfect for me.

While I am a detail-oriented person I much prefer to let my instincts take over. i.e. building a set to exact measurements and specifications is satisfying, but destroying it by kicking down walls, tearing pieces off or smashing through materials is much more fun.

After our very first performance together in Pordenone, he saw that in me, and saw that I was very comfortable on stage. He then got me an axe and an oil drum and a pig’s head for the VOD Fest. Then I felt like the Tasmanian Devil just waiting for the signal.

Karo: Your performances can be almost frightening in their intensity, yet there’s also something playful about your approach to extremes. Do you ever find yourself having an enormous amount of fun while the audience is experiencing something almost terrifying?

Robert: I’m always having a great time. The extreme expression is very comfortable for me.

There was a moment at WIF where there was a disagreement in the front row between a man and a woman. I was thrashing around and yelling but as soon as I saw a man yelling at a woman I was present and tried my best to escalate the situation.

The people I know that experience extreme emotions are comfortable there and have a lifetime of practice in controlling them.

Karo: Between your own recordings, The SPKtR, theatre and all the different forms of music you’ve explored, you’ve already created an extraordinary amount of work. Is there something you still haven’t made that you would genuinely regret leaving unrealised?

Robert: I love and appreciate this question. There are artists whose responses I’d love to hear. For me however, it requires ego that I’ve tried very hard to rid myself of.

Also, the distance between ideation and creation is very short for me, in terms of timeline. Creation starts in planning so that the execution is streamlined.

If I can empty my cup of a need to create, by creating as often as possible then my desires are revealed to be ego feeding. Creation is the point.

Whether it’s “good enough” upon listening back is an attempt at measuring oneself against what we think we should be. Maybe one day when I’m perfect, I’ll care.

Karo: The Wrocław performance provoked some strong reactions, including criticism that became quite personal. How do you respond when judgments about the music turn into judgments about the people making it?

Robert: There are things in my life that are so fundamentally important. Things I would die for. Things I would kill for. Things for which I would suffer a thousand slow deaths. Things I would do unspeakable evils to protect. And they are people. My Wife, my Children, my Family, my Loved ones. Anyone who knows me, knows that I mean every word of this, and I am more than capable of executing it with excruciating longevity.

By comparison, everything else falls so far short. The uninformed opinion of a stranger? Laughable.

I’ve seen people posting a sentiment over the years that “Industrial used to be dangerous” and “artists used to take risks”. That’s exactly what The SPKtR is doing in every way. Nothing is the same old shit. Everything is a new creation and some of it is rocky to coordinate.

If people have a problem with that then great. Not one of those people has offered a suggestion of what would be a better performance. Just complaints.

There are very few people around today who were actually at the old SPK shows and there’s a romanticized version in their heads of everything being so perfect and that everyone loved it. I’ve been told by someone who was at every single SPK gig that that’s not the case.

So when people have a reaction to The SPKtR it’s actually closer to the reactions that they got all those years ago. Some love, some hate, some appreciation and some disgust. My Dad has literal scars to prove it.

So while the material has changed in 40 years, the experience is actually closer to what it was.

About Robert J. Revell

Robert J. Revell is an Australian-born musician, composer and multidisciplinary artist from Sydney, currently based in Los Angeles. His work encompasses industrial music, experimental electronics, noise, musique concrète, metal, sound composition and performance art.

A multi-instrumentalist with experience as a guitarist, vocalist, bassist and drummer, Revell has performed and recorded across numerous genres, including death metal, thrash, doom, jazz, blues and experimental music. Alongside his musical activities, he builds theatre sets, combining carpentry, welding and mechanical engineering skills with an interest in physical structures and the processes of creation and destruction.

His debut solo album, “Torn Remnants of Nobility”, was released by Austrian experimental label Klanggalerie on 8 November 2025. The six-track recording explores difficult psychological territory through abrasive electronics, extreme instrumental textures and compositions concerned with violence, shame, guilt, regret and the possibility of emotional release. Revell wrote, recorded, mixed and created the artwork for the album himself.

Despite maintaining an extensive archive of approximately twenty largely unreleased albums, as well as music for film, television and theatre, Revell has generally approached composition as a personal necessity rather than a means of pursuing commercial recognition.

He is also a member of The SPKtR, the contemporary incarnation of SPK, the first-wave industrial project founded by his father, Graeme Revell. Their collaboration brings together Graeme’s compositional and technological approach with Robert’s instinctive, physically demanding performance style. In 2025, father and son appeared together in Pordenone, Italy, and at the Vinyl-on-Demand Festival. Their collaboration subsequently developed into the extensive European tour undertaken in November and December 2026, including their appearance at the 25th anniversary of Wrocław Industrial Festival.
